231:## Contradictions
233:- **C1 Fine-tuned vs GPT-4.** Fine-tuned AIBugHunter (F1 94%) and CodeBERT (87%) far exceed prompted gpt-4 (29%) on Big-Vul [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4], but GPT-4 CoT beats every fine-tuned model on pair-wise correctness on 564 PrimeVul pairs (12.94% vs ≤3.01%) [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9]. Differs in metric (F1 vs P-C), data (noisy random-split Big-Vul 1:20 vs de-duplicated time-split pairs) and model versions; Ding's own BigVul rows (F1 62.88–68.26%) agree with Fu [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7]. [I] Fine-tuned models exploit dataset artefacts rewarded by random splits [@risse2025top, p. 11]; on pairs all are below the 22.70% random reference, so the reversal reflects the benchmark more than the model family. Pass 2: on 1549 unpaired PrimeVul functions a fine-tuned CodeBERT-PrimeVul beats all 8 zero-shot LLMs (balanced accuracy 0.765 vs ≤0.711) [@deininger2026open, p. 11; @deininger2026open, p. 17]; with an argmax decision rule the same detector looks like always-safe (0.500) despite ROC-AUC 0.845 [@deininger2026open, p. 11]. [I] A conservative threshold is consistent with Ding's fine-tuned models labelling both pair members benign in 84–88% of pairs [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9]; unpaired and pair-wise results must not be pooled.
235:- **C3 LLM vs SAST.** LLMs win on 10 small C# projects [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10] and CASTLE C micro-programs [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 11]; CodeQL beats the best LLM's accuracy on OWASP, Juliet Java and Juliet C/C++ [@khare2025understanding, p. 9]; at repository level LLMs detect more but flag up to 77.4% of functions [@zhou2024comparison, p. 7] (preprint), and general agents lead recall while specialised LLM detectors and SAST show near-zero recall on some CWEs and 75–100% SFDR [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 11]. Differs in language, unit, synthetic vs real code, and scoring leniency (location rule only for LLMs [@gnieciak2025large, p. 6]; CASTLE prompt reveals scoring [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 9]). [I] Synthetic suites match SAST rules, small programs fit LLM context, real repositories defeat both: no single winner. Pass 2: on the same 1549 PrimeVul functions LLMs lead on balanced accuracy, but at 1:44 prevalence Flawfinder (6.2–13.4%) and Semgrep (26.0%, CI 5.7–66.9) are more precise than every LLM (2.3–4.6%), while Cppcheck sits in the LLM range [@deininger2026open, p. 8; @deininger2026open, p. 10]. [I] The families fail in opposite directions (LLMs over-flag, SAST finds little), so the ranking depends on the metric.
236:- **C4 Does reasoning reduce false positives?** For: reasoning models "consistently produced fewer false positives" [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 14]; RepoAudit precision 82.35–88.46% with reasoning backbones [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 16]. Against: DeepSeek R1 166 FP vs GPT-4o 116 in CASTLE's own table [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 11]; thinking raises F1 via recall with unchanged accuracy and turns negative under DA/MA [@tan2026think, p. 6; @tan2026think, p. 8]; reasoning LLMs near chance on REEF [@shu2026evaluating, p. 37]. [I] Holds for OpenAI o-series in some settings only. Pass 2, against: reasoning lowers DeepSeek-V3.2 specificity from 0.52 to 0.37 [@deininger2026open, p. 17; @deininger2026open, p. 20], while it helps frontier models' balanced accuracy. [I] Model-dependent.
237:- **C5 Class balance flips rankings.** Balanced REEF: fine-tuned GPT-4o + few-shot beats CodeT5P (Acc 0.7196 vs 0.6037) [@shu2026evaluating, p. 17]; imbalanced test: PLMs win (UniXcoder F1 0.4626 vs GPT-4o 0.4010) [@shu2026evaluating, p. 40; @shu2026evaluating, p. 41]. yildiz F1 drops from ~49–65% on balanced pairs to 5.41–12.21% on non-paired PrimeVul [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 7]. [I] Balanced sets reward liberal flagging; balanced rankings do not transfer to deployment. Pass 2: deininger's precision ranking at 1:44 differs from its balanced-accuracy ranking [@deininger2026open, p. 8]; in tashenova changing how negatives are drawn flips the majority class and the direction in which the same Random Forest fails [@tashenova2026real, p. 9].
239:- **C7 Same model, same benchmark, different in-distribution score.** LineVul (CodeBERT) trained and tested on BigVul: F1 91.00 [@lu2025lab, p. 12] vs CodeBERT BV→BV F1 62.88 [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7]. Neither paper explains the 28-point gap. [I] Likely split and preprocessing differences (lu used LineVul's original pipeline [@lu2025lab, p. 8]); in-distribution BigVul numbers are not comparable across papers.
240:- **C8 Does a time-split fine-tuned detector survive?** CodeBERT-PrimeVul on PrimeVul's chronologically later test split keeps balanced accuracy 0.765 (F1 ≈ 0.15 at 1:44, our calculation) [@deininger2026open, p. 11], while BigVul/ICVul/Devign/Juliet-trained DL on post-May-2025 VentiVul falls to F1 3.47–8.65 [@lu2025lab, p. 13]. [I] Differences in dataset (VentiVul 2025 CVEs, Whole-File units), training data quality (PrimeVul vs BigVul) and threshold policy; unresolved.
242:## Agreements / converging evidence
243:- **G1 Realistic evaluation collapses performance (strong).** DL precision falls to 1–10% on Real-Vul [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 7]; code-LM F1 62.88–68.26% → 18.05–21.43% within PrimeVul and 1.91–5.82% cross-dataset [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7]; LLM accuracy 10.5% lower on real-world than synthetic [@khare2025understanding, p. 5]; line-level F1 0.6641 → 0.3450 on 2024–25 code [@shu2026evaluating, p. 39]; statement-level scoring halves F1 [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 8]. Surveys concur [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 39; @sheng2025llms, p. 20]. Pass 2: on post-May-2025 CVEs at 1.97% prevalence, DL F1 3.47–8.65 and 7 of 12 LLM conservative F1 values fall below the all-positive F1 of 3.87% [@lu2025lab, p. 13; @lu2025lab, p. 14]; at 1:44, LLM precision 2.3–4.6% vs flag-all 2.21% [@deininger2026open, p. 8; @deininger2026open, p. 17]; on real WordPress PHP CVEs best macro-F1 0.601 [@tashenova2026real, p. 8].
244:- **G2 Benchmark labels are noisy (strong).** Independent audits: 39–65% of vulnerable labels correct [@risse2025top, p. 8]; 24–36% [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4]; ReVeal 15% inconsistency [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 3]. (The 25% BigVul figure is Chen et al. via Ding — not independent.) Pass 2: only 48.8% of cleaned positive WordPress-PHP labels are genuine (single annotator, n = 400) [@tashenova2026real, p. 11].
252:- **G10 Trivial baselines are competitive (moderate).** A one-feature token-count baseline matches or beats TF-IDF RF in 4/6 settings and is within 0.006 of the best neural model [@tashenova2026real, p. 8]; always-vulnerable F1 0.523 vs LLM F1 0.405–0.615 [@deininger2026open, p. 7]; all-positive F1 3.87% vs most LLM F1 on VentiVul [@lu2025lab, p. 14]; shu2026evaluating also reports all-vulnerable and all-clean dummy baselines [@shu2026evaluating, p. 11]. [I] Few papers report such baselines; most headline numbers are never compared to one.
253:- **G11 Cost per true positive (moderate, single study).** USD 0.003 (Gemma-3-4B) to 0.212 (Claude Sonnet 5) and 3.7–119.6 kJ per true positive at 1:44, excluding human triage of 25.6–41.9 false positives per true one [@deininger2026open, p. 8]; Qwen/Llama kJ/TP use FLOP estimates, not measured energy [@deininger2026open, p. 14].

[I] Fine-tuned models exploit dataset artefacts rewarded by random splits [@risse2025top, p. 11]; on pairs all are below the 22.70% random reference, so the reversal reflects the benchmark more than the model family. Pass 2: on 1549 unpaired PrimeVul functions a fine-tuned CodeBERT-PrimeVul beats all 8 zero-shot LLMs (balanced accuracy 0.765 vs ≤0.711) [@deininger2026open, p. 11; @deininger2026open, p. 17]; with an argmax decision rule the same detector looks like always-safe (0.500) despite ROC-AUC 0.845 [@deininger2026open, p. 11]. [I] A conservative threshold is consistent with Ding's fine-tuned models labelling both pair members benign in 84–88% of pairs [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9]; unpaired and pair-wise results must not be pooled.
- **C2 RepoAudit.** Own paper: 40 TP / 11 FP (78.43% precision), all 21 known bugs reproduced, $2.54 and 0.44 h per project [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 7; @guo2025repoaudit, p. 8]. Independent study: 0/110 known C/C++ vulnerabilities [@li2026llm, p. 7], 92.77% SFDR on real-world projects [@li2026llm, p. 11], average $172.77 per project, max $1,247.66 [@li2026llm, p. 16]. Differs in targets (prior tools' bug reports vs ReposVul CVEs), version (old commits vs current HEAD; the 5 overlapping modules only in li's real-world set), metric (precision vs recall/SFDR), labeller (authors vs Codex), bug types and scale. [I] Dependence on source/sink API coverage (zero-token runs; API modelling explains 108/108 misses [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 16]). Unresolved.
- **C3 LLM vs SAST.** LLMs win on 10 small C# projects [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10] and CASTLE C micro-programs [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 11]; CodeQL beats the best LLM's accuracy on OWASP, Juliet Java and Juliet C/C++ [@khare2025understanding, p. 9]; at repository level LLMs detect more but flag up to 77.4% of functions [@zhou2024comparison, p. 7] (preprint), and general agents lead recall while specialised LLM detectors and SAST show near-zero recall on some CWEs and 75–100% SFDR [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 11]. Differs in language, unit, synthetic vs real code, and scoring leniency (location rule only for LLMs [@gnieciak2025large, p. 6]; CASTLE prompt reveals scoring [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 9]). [I] Synthetic suites match SAST rules, small programs fit LLM context, real repositories defeat both: no single winner. Pass 2: on the same 1549 PrimeVul functions LLMs lead on balanced accuracy, but at 1:44 prevalence Flawfinder (6.2–13.4%) and Semgrep (26.0%, CI 5.7–66.9) are more precise than every LLM (2.3–4.6%), while Cppcheck sits in the LLM range [@deininger2026open, p. 8; @deininger2026open, p. 10]. [I] The families fail in opposite directions (LLMs over-flag, SAST finds little), so the ranking depends on the metric.
- **C4 Does reasoning reduce false positives?** For: reasoning models "consistently produced fewer false positives" [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 14]; RepoAudit precision 82.35–88.46% with reasoning backbones [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 16]. Against: DeepSeek R1 166 FP vs GPT-4o 116 in CASTLE's own table [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 11]; thinking raises F1 via recall with unchanged accuracy and turns negative under DA/MA [@tan2026think, p. 6; @tan2026think, p. 8]; reasoning LLMs near chance on REEF [@shu2026evaluating, p. 37]. [I] Holds for OpenAI o-series in some settings only. Pass 2, against: reasoning lowers DeepSeek-V3.2 specificity from 0.52 to 0.37 [@deininger2026open, p. 17; @deininger2026open, p. 20], while it helps frontier models' balanced accuracy. [I] Model-dependent.
- **C5 Class balance flips rankings.** Balanced REEF: fine-tuned GPT-4o + few-shot beats CodeT5P (Acc 0.7196 vs 0.6037) [@shu2026evaluating, p. 17]; imbalanced test: PLMs win (UniXcoder F1 0.4626 vs GPT-4o 0.4010) [@shu2026evaluating, p. 40; @shu2026evaluating, p. 41]. yildiz F1 drops from ~49–65% on balanced pairs to 5.41–12.21% on non-paired PrimeVul [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 7]. [I] Balanced sets reward liberal flagging; balanced rankings do not transfer to deployment. Pass 2: deininger's precision ranking at 1:44 differs from its balanced-accuracy ranking [@deininger2026open, p. 8]; in tashenova changing how negatives are drawn flips the majority class and the direction in which the same Random Forest fails [@tashenova2026real, p. 9].
- **C6 IRIS hybrid.** IRIS+GPT-4 beats CodeQL on 120 Java CVEs (55 vs 27; AvgFDR 84.82% vs 90.03%) [@li2024iris, p. 8], but on real-world Java IRIS SFDR is 97.80% vs CodeQL 77.00% [@li2026llm, p. 12]. Not like-for-like (known CVEs vs new code; detections vs SFDR; labelling). [I] Hybrids may raise recall on benchmark CVEs while adding noise on unseen code. Open.
- **C7 Same model, same benchmark, different in-distribution score.** LineVul (CodeBERT) trained and tested on BigVul: F1 91.00 [@lu2025lab, p. 12] vs CodeBERT BV→BV F1 62.88 [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7]. Neither paper explains the 28-point gap. [I] Likely split and preprocessing differences (lu used LineVul's original pipeline [@lu2025lab, p. 8]); in-distribution BigVul numbers are not comparable across papers.
- **C8 Does a time-split fine-tuned detector survive?** CodeBERT-PrimeVul on PrimeVul's chronologically later test split keeps balanced accuracy 0.765 (F1 ≈ 0.15 at 1:44, our calculation) [@deininger2026open, p. 11], while BigVul/ICVul/Devign/Juliet-trained DL on post-May-2025 VentiVul falls to F1 3.47–8.65 [@lu2025lab, p. 13]. [I] Differences in dataset (VentiVul 2025 CVEs, Whole-File units), training data quality (PrimeVul vs BigVul) and threshold policy; unresolved.

## Agreements / converging evidence
- **G1 Realistic evaluation collapses performance (strong).** DL precision falls to 1–10% on Real-Vul [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 7]; code-LM F1 62.88–68.26% → 18.05–21.43% within PrimeVul and 1.91–5.82% cross-dataset [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7]; LLM accuracy 10.5% lower on real-world than synthetic [@khare2025understanding, p. 5]; line-level F1 0.6641 → 0.3450 on 2024–25 code [@shu2026evaluating, p. 39]; statement-level scoring halves F1 [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 8]. Surveys concur [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 39; @sheng2025llms, p. 20]. Pass 2: on post-May-2025 CVEs at 1.97% prevalence, DL F1 3.47–8.65 and 7 of 12 LLM conservative F1 values fall below the all-positive F1 of 3.87% [@lu2025lab, p. 13; @lu2025lab, p. 14]; at 1:44, LLM precision 2.3–4.6% vs flag-all 2.21% [@deininger2026open, p. 8; @deininger2026open, p. 17]; on real WordPress PHP CVEs best macro-F1 0.601 [@tashenova2026real, p. 8].
- **G2 Benchmark labels are noisy (strong).** Independent audits: 39–65% of vulnerable labels correct [@risse2025top, p. 8]; 24–36% [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4]; ReVeal 15% inconsistency [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 3]. (The 25% BigVul figure is Chen et al. via Ding — not independent.) Pass 2: only 48.8% of cleaned positive WordPress-PHP labels are genuine (single annotator, n = 400) [@tashenova2026real, p. 11].
- **G3 Prompted LLMs over-flag and cannot separate vulnerable from patched code (moderate).** GPT-4 two-shot labels both pair members vulnerable in 71.63% of pairs [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9]; "both vulnerable" is 40–95% of failures [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 8]; dual-agent flags 88.2% [@tan2026think, p. 7]; always-vulnerable rows among khare's best F1 [@khare2025understanding, p. 16]. Partly one dataset family (PrimeVul).
- **G4 SAST recall is low on real code, high only on synthetic suites (moderate).** Best single tools 30.0–44.4%, many 0% [@zhou2024comparison, p. 6]; CodeQL recall 6.00–34.29% C/C++ and 14.19% Java [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 9]; CodeQL 27/120 on CWE-Bench-Java [@li2024iris, p. 8]; CASTLE CodeQL 29%, SAST average 23% [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 12]; vs CodeQL accuracy 0.94 on Juliet Java [@khare2025understanding, p. 9].
- **G5 CodeQL on OWASP replicates across groups (moderate).** P 0.58 / R 0.96 / F1 0.72 [@khare2025understanding, p. 9] vs P 60.3% / R 97.0% / F1 74.4% [@xiong2026sifting, p. 11].
- **G6 Missing context is the shared failure cause (moderate).** All 151 truly vulnerable audited functions need external context [@risse2025top, p. 9]; context-type identification ≤41.33% [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 9]; API modelling explains 108/108 RepoAudit (GPT-5.4) misses [@li2026llm, p. 7]; 14.60% of FPs from truncated inter-procedural context [@li2026llm, p. 15].
- **G7 LLM filtering of SAST alarms trades large FP reduction for lost true positives (moderate).** du2026reducing removes 94–98% of false alarms with real-bug recall 0.75–0.88 [@du2026reducing, p. 8] (own method, Tencent authors, non-security bugs); xiong2026sifting FPR 6.3% with 22.25% miss rate [@xiong2026sifting, p. 12; @xiong2026sifting, p. 18].
- **G8 Prompt-only LLMs trail adapted models (moderate).** Fine-tuned models beat prompted ChatGPT on Big-Vul [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4]; GPT-3.5 prompting detects 3.7–23.2% vs 89.2% fine-tuned CodeBERT [@zhou2024comparison, p. 10]; prompt-only LLMs near chance on REEF [@shu2026evaluating, p. 17].
- **G9 LLM cost far exceeds SAST and varies by orders of magnitude (moderate).** RepoAudit averages $172.77 per project [@li2026llm, p. 16]; alarm filtering < $0.20 per alarm [@du2026reducing, p. 8; @xiong2026sifting, p. 17]; GPT-4o instruction tuning ~15× a PLM run [@shu2026evaluating, p. 42].
- **G10 Trivial baselines are competitive (moderate).** A one-feature token-count baseline matches or beats TF-IDF RF in 4/6 settings and is within 0.006 of the best neural model [@tashenova2026real, p. 8]; always-vulnerable F1 0.523 vs LLM F1 0.405–0.615 [@deininger2026open, p. 7]; all-positive F1 3.87% vs most LLM F1 on VentiVul [@lu2025lab, p. 14]; shu2026evaluating also reports all-vulnerable and all-clean dummy baselines [@shu2026evaluating, p. 11]. [I] Few papers report such baselines; most headline numbers are never compared to one.
- **G11 Cost per true positive (moderate, single study).** USD 0.003 (Gemma-3-4B) to 0.212 (Claude Sonnet 5) and 3.7–119.6 kJ per true positive at 1:44, excluding human triage of 25.6–41.9 false positives per true one [@deininger2026open, p. 8]; Qwen/Llama kJ/TP use FLOP estimates, not measured energy [@deininger2026open, p. 14].

17	
18	# Open or Frontier? A Cost- and Energy-Aware Benchmark of Large Language Models for Software Vulnerability Detection
19	
20	- Authors: Deininger, Patrick; Slany, Wolfgang
21	- Year / venue: 2026, Computers (published)
22	- DOI: 10.3390/computers15090623 · URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/computers15090623
23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
24	
25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
26	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
27	
28	## 1. Research objective
29	[A] To benchmark open-weight against frontier LLMs on function-level vulnerability detection, treating monetary cost and energy as "first-class axes alongside detection quality" (p. 1). The study also calibrates the LLM results against non-LLM reference points (static analysers and learned detectors) "to gauge absolute difficulty" (p. 2). [A] The authors claim the conjunction is new (a security task, a five-model open roster, and cost and energy as per-task axes), stating "We make no claim to be first on any single one of these axes" (p. 3).
30	
31	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
32	- [V] No numbered RQs. Contributions are framed as (p. 2):
33	  - a cost- and energy-aware open-vs-frontier benchmark on label-clean PrimeVul with non-LLM reference points;
34	  - evidence on the quality–efficiency Pareto frontier;
35	  - an account of what can and cannot be measured for closed API models.
36	- [I] Implicit questions:
37	  1. Are open-weight LLMs competitive with frontier LLMs in quality?
38	  2. Are they more cost- and energy-efficient?
39	  3. How do LLMs compare with SAST and fine-tuned detectors at realistic prevalence?
40	
41	## 3. Methodology
42	- Research design: [V] Empirical benchmark of binary function-level detection ("does this C/C++ function contain a vulnerability?") on a fixed stratified PrimeVul sample (p. 4). Additional analyses (pp. 9–20):
43	  - re-scoring at the natural 1:44 prevalence;
44	  - configuration-matched families A/B/C;
45	  - prompt, sample-draw and run-to-run robustness;
46	  - a reasoning-vs-direct replication across two measurement epochs.
47	- Approach / model / intervention: [V] Eight LLMs prompted zero-shot through a unified OpenAI-compatible API gateway (p. 4, Table 2). [V] The gateway is **not named** (pp. 4, 29).
48	  - **Frontier:** Claude Sonnet 5, GPT-5.1, Gemini 3.1 Pro (`gemini-3.1-pro-preview`); active parameters assumed ~100B for the energy estimate.
49	  - **Open-weight:** DeepSeek-V3.2 (~37B active), GLM-5 (~32B active), Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen3-Coder-30B (3B active MoE), Gemma-3-4B.
50	  - [V] Pinned providers and precision: DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5 at GMICloud FP8; Llama-3.3-70B at DeepInfra FP8; Qwen3-Coder-30B at SiliconFlow FP8; Gemma-3-4B at DeepInfra bf16 (p. 29, Table A2).
51	  - [V] Main configuration: direct answer, reasoning disabled where permitted. Gemini cannot disable reasoning (HTTP 400) (p. 4, p. 29).
52	  - [V] Prompt: a security-reviewer persona; answer YES/NO first, then an optional explanation (p. 28). A lenient parser counts unparseable outputs as parse failures, not "safe" (p. 4, p. 29).
53	- Baselines or comparison conditions:
54	  - [V] **Trivial baselines:** always-safe and always-vulnerable (p. 7, Table 4); always-flag at 1:44 prevalence (p. 8, Table 5).
55	  - [V] **SAST arm** (p. 6, p. 10, Table 7): Flawfinder 2.0.20 (lexical), Cppcheck 2.21 (flow-sensitive), Semgrep 1.175 with community C and security-audit rulesets (pattern plus intraprocedural taint). A function is flagged if any finding reaches a swept severity threshold.
56	  - [V] **DL arm:**
57	    - CodeBERT fine-tuned on Devign (off the shelf, cross-dataset, argmax, 512 tokens) (p. 6);
58	    - CodeBERT (125M) fine-tuned on PrimeVul's training split, with the threshold selected on the validation split (p. 10–11).
59	  - [V] **CodeQL was not run.** PrimeVul functions are isolated snippets with no build, so no CodeQL database can be built (p. 10–11).
60	
61	## 4. Dataset and sample
62	- Data source(s): [V] PrimeVul test split (C/C++): 24,788 functions after loading, 549 vulnerable — "a realistic 1:44 class ratio" (p. 4).
63	  - [I] This differs from the PrimeVul test split recorded in ding2025vulnerability (695 vulnerable / 25,216 benign) [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 6]. The paper does not explain the difference beyond "after loading" (p. 4); filtering or de-duplication on load is plausible but not reported.
64	- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] N = 1549 functions: all 549 vulnerable plus 1000 seeded-random safe functions (p. 4). [I] Prevalence in the evaluated sample is 35.4% (549/1549). This is **not** 50/50, although the text once calls it "balanced by construction" (p. 8). [V] The effective N per model is 1526–1549 because parse failures are excluded (p. 6).
65	- Sampling / selection method:
66	  - [V] Label-stratified sample fixed by seed (p. 4).
67	  - [V] Two further near-disjoint safe pools (<6% overlap) were drawn for robustness (p. 19).
68	  - [V] LLM inputs were truncated to 8000 characters. This affects 105/1549 functions and 87/549 (15.8%) of the vulnerable ones (p. 4).
69	  - [A] "The two non-LLM baselines" see the untruncated function and are therefore "if anything, advantaged" on long inputs (p. 4). [V] But the CodeBERT-Devign baseline uses "inputs truncated to 512 tokens" (p. 6); the input length of CodeBERT-PrimeVul is not reported (pp. 10–11).
70	  - [I] The untruncated claim can hold only for the SAST tools. CodeBERT's 512-token window is shorter than the LLMs' 8000-character budget, so on long functions CodeBERT is, if anything, disadvantaged — which strengthens rather than weakens its win over the LLMs (basis: p. 4, p. 6; CodeBERT-PrimeVul's limit inferred from the architecture, not reported).
71	  - [V] All CVEs date from 2008–2022 and predate the models' training cutoffs (p. 24). [V] The PrimeVul training split contains no evaluated function or function body (up to whitespace) (p. 10, p. 25).
72	- Data availability (public? link?): [V] Released on Zenodo (doi 10.5281/zenodo.21391073): harness, configurations, sampled function IDs, price snapshot, energy sweep, baseline scores and aggregated results (p. 26). [V] PrimeVul is fetched from its original authors by script; the fine-tuned checkpoint is regenerable by script (p. 26).
73	
74	## 5. Experimental setup
75	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools:
76	  - [V] Harness and decoding: a test-driven harness with 82 automated tests; temperature 0, seed 12345, one generation per item; output budget 64 tokens in the matched configuration (256 for two frontier models in the first epoch) (p. 6, p. 29).
77	  - [V] Cost: computed from logged input/output tokens × list price at a pinned provider, with gateway fallbacks disabled (p. 5).
78	  - [V] Provider price dispersion: up to 14.4× for DeepSeek-V3.2 (USD 0.209–3.000 per million input tokens) (p. 5, Table 3).
79	  - [V] Energy (p. 5):
80	    - FLOP estimate E ≈ 2·N_active·T·ε for API-served models;
81	    - measured with the NVML energy counter on a dedicated NVIDIA H200 for locally servable open models (concurrency 1, idle-subtracted "active" energy);
82	    - plus a concurrency sweep c = 1/8/32/64 (p. 14, Table 9).
83	  - [V] Latency: client-side under concurrency 10, so it conflates queueing (p. 30).
84	  - [V] Statistics: stratified paired bootstrap of balanced-accuracy differences (20,000 resamples, seed 12,345) with Holm correction over a 9-comparison primary family and a 15-comparison strict family (p. 6, p. 28).
85	- Code availability: [V] The harness and configurations are released (p. 6, p. 26).
86	
87	## 6. Evaluation metrics
88	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
89	  - [V] **Balanced accuracy** is the primary metric, because accuracy is dominated by the always-safe classifier (0.646 accuracy, above every LLM) and both trivial classifiers score exactly 0.5 on it (p. 6).
90	  - [V] MCC and F1 are also reported (p. 6).
91	  - [V] Deployment metrics at 1:44 prevalence are derived from the prevalence-invariant TPR/FPR (p. 8, Table 5):
92	    - precision; false positives per true positive (FP/TP);
93	    - alerts and found vulnerabilities per 1000 functions;
94	    - **USD per true positive** and **kJ per true positive**.
95	  - [V] Elicited 0–100 confidence gives ROC-AUC where usable. VD-Score is declined because the coarse score grids cannot reach its 0.5% FPR point (p. 9–10).
96	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals):
97	  - [V] Paired bootstrap 95% CIs and Holm-adjusted p for open-vs-frontier gaps (p. 27, Table A1).
98	  - [V] Wilson-based 95% CIs on precision at deployment prevalence for the non-LLM baselines (p. 10, Table 7).
99	  - [V] Robustness: Spearman rank correlation across prompts and draws (p. 19, Table 13).
100	  - [V] Output-budget effects are tested with a paired bootstrap (p. 16, Table 10).
101	
102	## 7. Key findings
103	1. **Detection quality, first epoch** — [V] Balanced accuracy / F1 per model, direct mode, N = 1549 (p. 7, Table 4). [V] F1 range across LLMs is 0.405–0.615 vs always-vulnerable F1 0.523 (p. 7, Table 4).
104	
105	   | Model | Bal. acc. (95% CI) | F1 |
106	   |---|---|---|
107	   | DeepSeek-V3.2 | 0.676 (0.654–0.697) | 0.615 |
108	   | Gemma-3-4B | 0.653 | 0.590 |
109	   | GLM-5 | 0.637 | 0.596 |
110	   | Gemini-3.1-Pro | 0.623 | 0.591 |
111	   | GPT-5.1 | 0.617 | 0.560 |
112	   | Claude-Sonnet-5 | 0.616 | 0.582 |
113	   | Llama-3.3-70B | 0.604 | 0.578 |
114	   | Qwen3-Coder-30B | 0.511 | 0.405 |
115	
116	2. **Open vs frontier significance** — [V] DeepSeek-V3.2 significantly beats all three frontier models: +0.054 to +0.060 balanced accuracy, Holm p < 5×10⁻⁴ (p. 6, p. 27, Table A1).
117	   - [V] Gemma-3-4B beats Claude-Sonnet-5 (+0.037, Holm p = 0.032); the other top-open gaps are not significant (p. 7, p. 27).
118	   - [V] Qwen3-Coder-30B is indistinguishable from chance (MCC 0.022, CI −0.03 to 0.07) (p. 7).
119	3. **Budget-matched second epoch (Family A)** — [V] Balanced accuracy / MCC: DeepSeek-V3.2 0.711 / 0.403; GLM-5 0.669 / 0.352; Gemma-3-4B 0.653 / 0.297; Claude-Sonnet-5 0.653 / 0.321; GPT-5.1 0.615 / 0.225; Llama 0.609 / 0.267; Qwen 0.568 / 0.136; Gemini 0.606 / 0.252, on only the 54.2% of tasks it answered (p. 17, Table 11).
120	   - [V] Claude equals Gemma (+0.0003, p = 0.98) (p. 17).
121	   - [V] Absolute numbers shifted by up to 0.06 between epochs seven weeks apart ("service drift") (p. 7–8, p. 20).
122	4. **Reasoning mode** — [V] Reasoning helps every frontier model (Claude +0.032, GPT-5.1 +0.044, Gemini +0.096) but hurts DeepSeek-V3.2 (−0.133, p < 10⁻⁴) and does not help GLM-5 (−0.019, n.s.); it costs 4.5–12.1× more per task (p. 17–18, Table 12).
123	   - [V] Best observed: DeepSeek 0.711 (direct) vs Claude 0.685 and Gemini 0.680 (reasoning); DeepSeek vs Claude p = 0.081 (p. 17).
124	   - [V] Reasoning lowers DeepSeek's specificity from 0.52 to 0.37 (p. 20).
125	5. **Prompt sensitivity dominates** — [V] Two paraphrases move balanced accuracy by up to 0.088 and produce three different winners (DeepSeek 0.711, Claude 0.741, GLM-5 0.700); Spearman ρ vs anchor = 0.381 and 0.810 (p. 19–20, Table 13).
126	   - [V] Safe-pool redraws move scores ≤0.015 (ρ = 1.000) (p. 19).
127	   - [V] Temperature-0 verdict agreement is 88.3–100%; only Gemma is exactly reproducible (p. 19).
128	6. **SAST baselines on the same functions** (p. 7, p. 10, Table 4, Table 7) — balanced accuracy / recall / specificity / precision at 1:44:
129	   - [V] Flawfinder risk≥1: 0.589 / 0.271 / 0.907 / 6.20%; risk≥4: 0.523 / 0.055 / 0.992 / 13.40%.
130	   - [V] Cppcheck: 0.548–0.592 balanced accuracy; precision 2.46–3.77%.
131	   - [V] Semgrep severity≥INFO: 0.514 / 0.031 / 0.998 / 25.96% (CI 5.7–66.9%). It flags 19 of 1549 functions with 17 TP and 2 FP (p. 11).

190	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
191	- [A] Energy is measured for only some open models; frontier energy rests on an untested active-parameter assumption and is reported as a sensitivity range (p. 23).
192	- [A] Configuration asymmetries: Gemini cannot run without reasoning; two frontier models needed larger output budgets in the main run (p. 24).
193	- [A] Latency is confounded by queueing (p. 24).
194	- [A] Training-data contamination: all CVEs are 2008–2022 and may appear in pre-training; a recall gradient by CVE year is "consistent with some memorization"; absolute scores "may be optimistic"; a post-cutoff restriction is planned (p. 24).
195	- [A] The fine-tuned CodeBERT-PrimeVul detector is in-distribution (trained on PrimeVul's own training split) while the LLMs are zero-shot; the authors call this "not an unfair comparison" but note the different prerequisites (several thousand labelled vulnerable functions vs none) (p. 11).
196	- [A] One prompt, one draw and one generation in the headline table; variation across datasets and task formulations remains unbounded (p. 24).
197	- [A] Serving-layer dependence (p. 24–25):
198	  - price spread up to 14×;
199	  - two silent serving faults: billed empty outputs, and a reasoning flag ignored with HTTP 200;
200	  - quality is robust to provider and precision for Llama (0.599–0.609).
201	- [A] CodeQL cannot be applied to unbuildable function snippets (p. 25).
202	- [A] Scope: one dataset, one task formulation, function level only; other languages and statement-level localisation are future work (p. 25).
203	- [A] "No result here should be read as evidence that function-level vulnerability triage is ready for independent use" (p. 26).

205	## 9. Limitations we identified
206	- [I] **Internal inconsistencies from revision** (the paper went through at least one major review round, p. 1, pp. 16–19):
207	  - Gemma-3-4B is said to be incompatible with the local vLLM/CUDA build, so its energy is FLOP-estimated (p. 6, p. 15). Yet Table 9 reports a measured concurrency sweep for Gemma (p. 14), and the abstract says three open models were measured (p. 1), while p. 5 says two.
208	  - The limitations list says a fine-tuned PrimeVul detector "is the remaining gap" (p. 25), but Section 4.4 reports exactly such a detector (p. 10–11).
209	  - The reasoning cost multiplier is "2.5 to 7.6 times" on p. 24, which refers to the earlier-epoch comparison of Section 4.9 (p. 20); Section 4.9 gives no cost table, so that range cannot be checked. Cite Table 12's 4.5–12.1× (p. 18) instead.
210	  - The sample is called "balanced by construction" (p. 8) although it is 35.4% positive (p. 4).
211	  - p. 2 says "every model we tested raises roughly twenty-six false alarms per true finding", but Table 5 gives 25.6–41.9 FP/TP; 25.6 is the best model only (p. 8). p. 21 attributes "roughly twenty-six" to "the best model".
212	  - p. 23 says the best open models "dominate the frontier on both the quality and the efficiency axes", whereas p. 21 says the data "do not support a general claim of quality dominance", and DeepSeek's lead over Claude in Family C is not significant (p = 0.081) (p. 17).
213	  - p. 4 speaks of "two non-LLM baselines (Section 3.4)", but Section 3.4 lists four non-LLM detectors (p. 6).
214	  - These are reporting slips, not evidence of wrong numbers, but readers should cite table values rather than prose.
215	- [I] **The SAST arm is weak by design for C/C++.** Flawfinder, Cppcheck and Semgrep community rules on isolated functions, with no CodeQL, Infer or commercial tools (p. 10–11). The comparison is LLM vs lightweight function-level SAST, not vs semantic whole-program SAST.
216	- [I] Contamination and the in-distribution vs zero-shot asymmetry are author-stated (§8, p. 11, p. 24). Our addition: both cut in different directions — contamination may inflate the LLM scores, while the asymmetry favours CodeBERT — so the size of CodeBERT's lead over zero-shot LLMs on genuinely unseen code is unknown.
217	- [I] **Cost per TP excludes triage.** With 25.6–41.9 FP per TP (p. 8), analyst time would dominate compute cost (cents per TP). The paper's USD/TP therefore understates the practical cost per confirmed vulnerability by a large factor.
218	- [I] **Unnamed gateway** and preview model identifiers (`gemini-3.1-pro-preview`, p. 29) limit long-term reproducibility. The service drift of up to 0.06 between epochs (p. 20) shows API results are time-stamped observations.
219	- [I] **Function-level, C/C++ only** — no repository context. The truncation at 8000 characters affects 15.8% of positives (p. 4).
220	- **AI-assisted writing and code.** [V] The authors used DeepL Translator and ChatGPT (GPT-5.5, OpenAI) "to translate words, phrases, and passages from German into English", and Claude (Opus 5 and Sonnet 5, Anthropic) "to assist with drafting and revising portions of the text and with writing Python code"; "no figures, data, or images were AI-generated or fabricated" (p. 27). [V] The harness is covered by 82 automated tests (p. 6).
221	  - [I] Both assisting vendors (OpenAI, Anthropic) also supply evaluated models (GPT-5.1, Claude-Sonnet-5; p. 4). The disclosure and the test suite reduce the concern; we note it for transparency, not as a conflict. Our own analysis pipeline is also Claude-based, which readers may wish to weigh when judging our reading of Claude results.

224	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection):
225	  - [V] Train/test separation for CodeBERT-PrimeVul is verified: no evaluated function or body is in training (p. 25).
226	  - [V] Thresholds are tuned on validation, not test (sweeping on test would give 0.777 vs the reported 0.765) (p. 11).
227	  - [V] Contamination is not controlled but is measured as a recall gradient by CVE year (p. 24).
228	  - [V] Epoch drift is handled by within-epoch comparisons (p. 16–18).
229	  - [V] Parse failures are excluded, not recoded (p. 27).

231	  - [V] One dataset (PrimeVul), C/C++, function level (p. 25).

258	## 12. Relevance to our research
259	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (primary: LLM vs SAST vs fine-tuned DL on identical functions), RQ2, RQ3 (cost/energy trade-offs; no hybrid), RQ5.
260	- How it informs our work [I]:
261	  - **RQ1:** one of very few same-benchmark three-family comparisons. The ranking depends on the metric:
262	    - on balanced accuracy: fine-tuned CodeBERT > best LLMs > Flawfinder/Cppcheck > Semgrep;
263	    - on precision at realistic prevalence: Semgrep (26.0%, 95% CI 5.7–66.9) and strict-threshold Flawfinder (13.4%) > CodeBERT (8.2%, CI 6.9–9.7) > lenient Flawfinder (6.2%) > all LLMs (2.3–3.8% first epoch, p. 8; 2.8–4.6% budget-matched, p. 17). Cppcheck (2.46–3.77%) sits in the LLM range (p. 10, Table 7). Only Flawfinder and Semgrep beat every LLM on precision, and the Semgrep and Flawfinder intervals overlap CodeBERT's, so their ordering against CodeBERT is not established (p. 10, Table 7);
264	    - all are far from deployable.
265	  - This fits our "LLMs higher recall, lower precision" pattern and C3/C5.
266	  - **Correction for our gap report.** The G2 and G6 novelty-check notes describe *Open or Frontier?* as "No SAST". That is **incorrect**: Flawfinder 2.0.20, Cppcheck 2.21 and Semgrep 1.175 are run on the identical 1549 functions (p. 6, p. 10). G2 is therefore narrowed further: a same-benchmark LLM + SAST + fine-tuned DL comparison now exists at function level on C/C++. What is still missing is post-cutoff code, repository level, and semantic SAST.
267	  - **G6 is narrowed further.** USD/TP and kJ/TP at 1:44 prevalence are reported for 8 LLMs (p. 8). The remaining gap is the triage-effort term and a costed SAST/DL arm (≈0 is not quantified per TP).
268	  - **G1:** a further study that reports trivial baselines and realistic-prevalence re-scoring. It shows LLM precision barely above always-flag (2.3–3.8% first epoch, 2.8–4.6% budget-matched, vs 2.21%; p. 8, p. 17).
269	  - **C1:** the argmax-collapse artefact (p. 11) suggests some reports of fine-tuned models being near chance on PrimeVul may reflect decision thresholds rather than ranking ability. This is a candidate explanation, not established for other papers.
270	  - **C4:** reasoning raises frontier balanced accuracy but lowers DeepSeek's specificity (more false positives) (p. 17, p. 20). This supports the "model-dependent" reading.

28	## 1. Research objective
29	- [A] Test whether DL vulnerability detectors and LLMs that score well on curated benchmarks still work under deployment-like conditions. The study looks at three things: separability of code representations, within- vs cross-dataset generalisation, and detection of recent, temporally separated vulnerabilities (p. 1, p. 2).
30	- [A] Contribution claimed: VentiVul, a temporally separated out-of-distribution (OOD) benchmark of 200 CVEs / 263 vulnerable–patched pairs, plus a "Whole-File" + "Function-Pair" evaluation protocol (p. 2). "Out-of-distribution" means test data drawn from a different source or period than the training data.
31	
32	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
33	- [A] RQ1: do graph-based and CodeBERT representations separate vulnerable from non-vulnerable code before task-specific training? (p. 6)
34	- [A] RQ2: how do benchmark characteristics affect within-dataset and cross-dataset performance of DL detectors? (p. 7)
35	- [A] RQ3: how well do trained DL models and off-the-shelf LLMs detect recent vulnerabilities on a temporally separated benchmark? (p. 7)
36	- No formal hypotheses.

38	## 3. Methodology
39	- Research design: [V] Controlled empirical evaluation in three stages: representation diagnostics (t-SNE + centroid distance), 4×4 train/test matrix of DL models across datasets, inference-only evaluation on VentiVul (pp. 6–8).
40	- Approach / models: [V] DL: Devign (gated GNN on code property graphs), ReVeal (Joern graphs + token embeddings, SMOTE), LineVul (fine-tuned CodeBERT), VulBERTa (RoBERTa pretrained on C/C++) (p. 5). LLMs, open-weight, no fine-tuning: Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite-Instruct (16B MoE, 2.4B active), Qwen3-30B-A3B (thinking mode disabled), Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct-2501, all released before May 2025 (p. 5, p. 8).
41	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] DL vs LLM only on VentiVul. Only ReVeal and LineVul (each trained on the four datasets) were taken to VentiVul; Devign and VulBERTa were not (p. 7). LLM prompting: zero-shot, few-shot (demonstrations drawn from complete vulnerable–patched pairs, the same number from each project; k = 4 is given only "for example", and the k actually used is not stated), chain-of-thought (p. 8, Table 4 p. 9). [I] No SAST tool, no proprietary/frontier LLM, no fine-tuned LLM and no trivial baseline (e.g. all-positive or random) is included.
42	
43	## 4. Dataset and sample
44	- Data source(s): [V] Juliet 253,002 functions, 37% vulnerable, synthetic; Devign 27,318, 46%, manual; BigVul 188,636, 6%, patches; ICVul 15,396, 41%, patches (p. 3, Table 1). All C/C++.
45	- VentiVul: [V] CVEs for Linux and Chromium disclosed from May 1, 2025, taken from NVD in disclosure order until 100 per project; manually verified; target size fixed before collection; "records were not selected based on model predictions" (p. 4). 13,326 functions, 200 CVEs, 39 CWEs, 263 pairs; Chromium 7,095 functions / 100 CVEs / 20 CWEs / 147 pairs; Linux 6,231 / 100 / 27 / 116 (p. 4, Table 2). Pre-fix function = vulnerable, post-fix = non-vulnerable, plus other functions from the same files labelled non-vulnerable to keep realistic imbalance (p. 4).
46	- Sample size (N) and unit: functions (Whole-File), CVEs (CDR) and vulnerable–patched pairs (PACC) (p. 7). [I] Each of the 263 pairs has exactly one vulnerable function (p. 4), so prevalence p = 263/13,326 = 1.97%. The Table 7 numbers confirm this: back-calculating prevalence from accuracy, precision and recall gives 1.97% for every LineVul row, which matches 263/13,326. The ReVeal rows give 1.79%, because ReVeal is scored only on the functions its preprocessing can handle (p. 7). An all-positive classifier would therefore score F1 = 2p/(1+p) ≈ 3.87% on the full set and ≈ 3.5% on ReVeal's subset (our calculation from p. 4 and Table 7 p. 13).
47	- Sampling / selection method: [V] Inclusion: valid references, explicit fix in non-test C/C++ files, CWE available; excluded: missing references, non-C/C++ or test-only fixes, fixes with "excessive unrelated files or functions" (p. 4). Train/test split ratios for the four benchmarks: not reported.
48	- Data availability: [V] "All of our datasets, code, and results are available" on GitHub (p. 2).
49	
50	## 5. Experimental setup
51	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] DL models use the original authors' code and "recommended settings" (p. 8); H100 GPUs (p. 8). Leakage controls: strict train–test splits with duplicate functions filtered, a fixed test set per target benchmark (p. 7). LLMs run locally via vLLM on B200 GPUs, temperature 0, top-p 1, seed 42, max 384 output tokens, JSON-only binary label; unparseable outputs kept as failures (p. 8). Each model, DL or LLM, receives one function at a time (p. 7, p. 8). Few-shot demonstrations are removed from the test set by pair identifier and code hash (p. 8). ReVeal metrics are computed only over functions its preprocessing can handle (p. 7). Two policies for LLMs: valid-only and conservative (failures counted wrong) (p. 8).
52	- Code availability: [V] public GitHub repository (p. 2).
53	
54	## 6. Evaluation metrics
55	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: [V] Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1 for Whole-File (p. 9). CVE Detection Rate (CDR): share of CVEs with at least one vulnerable function flagged, i.e. CVE-level coverage (p. 9). Patch Pair Accuracy (PACC): share of pairs where the vulnerable version is flagged and the patched version is not, i.e. sensitivity to the fix (p. 9). Centroid distance in min-max normalised t-SNE space, described as descriptive only (pp. 8–9).
56	- Statistical testing: not reported. There are no significance tests or confidence intervals. LLMs use one deterministic run (temperature 0, seed 42, p. 8). For DL training, the number of runs and the random seeds are not reported (p. 8 refers only to the original authors' "recommended settings").
57	
58	## 7. Key findings
59	1. In-distribution DL (within-dataset) — [V] LineVul F1 94.52 and VulBERTa 94.14 on Juliet; LineVul F1 91.00 on BigVul (p. 11; Table 6 p. 12). On BigVul, ReVeal, Devign and VulBERTa reach accuracy 87.45, 94.09, 94.39 but F1 only 23.58, 16.90, 0.19 (p. 11). [A] Because BigVul has a much smaller vulnerable share (6%), "predictions biased toward the non-vulnerable majority class can produce high accuracy while detecting few vulnerable functions" (p. 11).
60	2. Cross-dataset DL — [V] LineVul (Juliet) F1 94.52 in-dataset falls to 53.95 (Devign), 10.73 (BigVul), 51.22 (ICVul) (p. 11). LineVul (BigVul) falls from 91.00 to 0 (Juliet), 1.90 (Devign), 13.05 (ICVul) (p. 12). ReVeal (BigVul) is below 1.00 F1 on all three external sets (p. 11). [A] "No evaluated model consistently preserves its within-dataset performance" (p. 11).
61	3. Temporally separated DL (VentiVul, Whole-File) — [V] F1 3.47–8.65 across the 8 ReVeal/LineVul configurations; best ReVeal (BigVul) F1 8.65 with precision 5.25%, recall 24.43% (p. 13, Table 7). Devign-trained models: recall 99.24–100% but precision about 2% (p. 13, Table 7). LineVul (BigVul) F1 6.87 on VentiVul vs 91.00 in-distribution (Table 7 p. 13; Table 6 p. 12).
62	4. Temporally separated LLMs (VentiVul) — [V] Conservative F1 0.79–5.36 across 4 models × 3 prompts; all conservative F1 < 5.5% and all PACC < 6% (p. 13; Table 8 p. 14). Best: Mistral-Small-24B few-shot F1 5.36%, CDR 46%, PACC 5.75% (p. 13). Highest valid-only F1: Qwen2.5-Coder-32B CoT 8.21% (conservative 3.04%) (p. 14, Table 8). Zero-shot conservative F1: Qwen2.5-Coder 3.72, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite 4.29, Qwen3 3.09, Mistral 4.07 (p. 14, Table 8). LLM precision and recall are not reported, and the LLMs have no in-distribution numbers.
63	5. DL vs LLM on VentiVul (mostly but not exactly the same samples) [V/I] — [V] best DL Whole-File F1 8.65 (ReVeal-BigVul) vs best LLM conservative F1 5.36 (Mistral few-shot) (p. 13; p. 14). Zero-shot LLM CDR (34%, 20%, 9%, 5%) is lower than most DL configurations (p. 13). Best PACC: DL 5.34% vs LLM 5.75% (p. 13). [V] The evaluated samples differ: ReVeal is scored only on functions it can process (p. 7), the few-shot test set excludes pairs used as demonstrations, and valid-only metrics use only parseable outputs (p. 8). [I] F1 against chance (all-positive F1 ≈ 3.87% at p = 1.97%; ≈ 3.5% on ReVeal's subset; §4): the best DL F1 of 8.65 is about 2.5× its chance level, while the best LLM F1 of 5.36 is about 1.4× chance. LineVul (Devign), with recall 100%, precision 2% and F1 3.93, is in effect the all-positive predictor (p. 13, Table 7). [I] PACC against chance: a random labeller that flags a fraction q of functions independently of their content would get PACC = q(1−q), up to 25% at q = 0.5. All observed PACC values (≤ 5.75%, DL and LLM) are far below that, which means the models usually give the vulnerable and the patched version the same label (our reasoning from the PACC definition, p. 9). This matches ding2025vulnerability, where random pair-wise correctness is 22.70% and models fall far below it [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9].
64	6. CDR vs PACC gap — [V] ReVeal (Devign), ReVeal (ICVul), LineVul (Devign) reach CDR 99.10%, 94.59%, 100% but PACC 0.76%, 0%, 0% (p. 13). [A] Detecting a vulnerable function "does not imply" telling it apart from its patch (p. 13).
65	7. Prompting — [V] Few-shot improves Mistral on all three metrics but degrades the other models; CoT raises Qwen2.5-Coder valid-only F1 but lowers its PACC (p. 13). [A] Prompting effects are "model- and metric-dependent" (p. 13).
66	8. Project/CWE variation — [V] All LLMs have higher CDR on Linux than Chromium. DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite zero-shot CDR is 26% on Chromium and 42% on Linux (p. 13). LineVul (BigVul) has CDR 76% on Chromium and 0 on Linux (p. 13). The LLM project-specific results are zero-shot, valid-only (p. 13). Best project-specific PACC is < 8% (LineVul-ICVul 7.48% on Chromium) (p. 14). Per-CWE PACC peaks at 18.18% (LineVul-ICVul, CWE-472) on small cells (p. 14).
67	9. Representations — [V] GNN centroid distances: Juliet 0.0242, ICVul 0.0057, BigVul 0.1612; CodeBERT: BigVul 0.166, Devign 0.0068 (pp. 9–10). [A] Neither representation consistently separates vulnerable from non-vulnerable code (p. 10).
68	
69	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
70	- [A] Only four DL models, two DL families on VentiVul, four open-weight LLMs; no proprietary LLMs; conclusions apply to the evaluated models (p. 17).
71	- [A] LLM pretraining corpora and cutoffs are unknown, so temporal separation "cannot fully exclude training-data contamination" (p. 17).
72	- [A] t-SNE is parameter-sensitive, and centroid distance cannot capture nonlinear structure. RQ1 does not establish a causal link to RQ2/RQ3 performance (p. 17, p. 15).
73	- [A] Dataset characteristics vary simultaneously, so individual causes cannot be isolated. Preprocessing drops some functions, which affects comparability (p. 17).
74	- [A] VentiVul is C/C++ only (Linux, Chromium) and may not generalise to other languages or proprietary code. "Unrelated" functions may hide other vulnerabilities (residual label noise), and regex function extraction can miss complex C/C++ syntax, which mainly affects Whole-File (p. 17).
75	- [A] VentiVul "does not contain every vulnerability reported for the selected project versions" (incomplete coverage) (p. 17).
76	- [A] Model coverage was constrained by reproducibility, experimental consistency and computational feasibility; conclusions apply "to the evaluated models and settings rather than to all existing vulnerability detection techniques" (p. 17).
77	- [A] The Function-Pair setting is "less exposed" to label-noise and extraction threats because it uses manually verified vulnerable functions and their patched versions (p. 17).
78	- [A] ICVul and VentiVul come from open-source projects and may not represent proprietary industrial software (p. 17).
79	
80	## 9. Limitations we identified
81	- [I] No trivial baseline. At p = 263/13,326 = 1.97% (p. 4), an all-positive classifier scores F1 = 2p/(1+p) ≈ 3.87%. All eight DL F1 values (3.47–8.65, Table 7 p. 13) are at most 4.8 points above that. Seven of the 12 LLM conservative F1 values (Table 8 p. 14) fall below it: 3.72, 2.95, 3.04, 3.64, 3.09, 0.79 and 1.39. The paper calls these results "limited" or "weak" (p. 13) but never compares them with chance.
82	- [I] The DL and LLM comparison is asymmetric. DL models were trained on historical data; LLMs were used zero/few-shot without fine-tuning, with small open-weight models (MoE models with 2.4–3B active parameters) and Qwen3 thinking disabled (p. 5, p. 8). The study says nothing about frontier or fine-tuned LLMs, and nothing about LLMs in-distribution, because LLMs were not run on the four benchmarks.
83	- [I] LLM precision/recall are not reported (Table 8 gives F1, CDR, PACC only, p. 14), so we cannot tell whether LLMs fail through false positives or false negatives.
84	- [I] No confidence intervals. LLMs get a single deterministic run (temperature 0, seed 42, p. 8); DL run counts and seeds are not reported. With 263 pairs, PACC differences of a few points (e.g. 5.34% vs 5.75%) are within noise.
85	- [I] One function at a time with no context (p. 7). This is fair between families but disadvantages LLMs, which may need inter-procedural context. With 263 pairs across 200 CVEs (p. 4), at most 63 CVEs have more than one affected function (e.g. CVE-2025-37777, two functions in two files, p. 4). The share of CVEs that need cross-function reasoning is not reported.
86	- [I] No static-analysis tool is evaluated, although the introduction positions learning-based detection as a complement to static analysis (p. 1).
87	- [I] Version: we analyse arXiv v4 (4 Nov 2026), the accepted manuscript (footnote p. 1). The published JSS version (doi 10.1016/j.jss.2026.113185, Crossref-verified 2026-11-12) is not open access and was not compared with it, so small differences between the two versions cannot be ruled out. Page refs follow arXiv v4.
88	
89	## 10. Threats to validity
90	- Internal: [I] Deduplication within datasets and fixed test sets are reported (p. 7), but split ratios and cross-dataset overlap checks are not reported (Devign is from FFmpeg/QEMU and BigVul from open-source C/C++ repositories, p. 3, so project overlap is possible but unchecked). ReVeal is scored only on functions it can process (p. 7), which may inflate or deflate its numbers relative to LineVul. Overlap with training and pretraining data was not checked. Temporal separation covers the CVEs and their fixes (disclosed from May 2025, p. 4). The "unrelated" same-file functions that make up most of VentiVul can be much older code. The paper describes BigVul and ICVul only as drawn from open-source C/C++ repositories and GitHub fix commits (p. 3), and does not say whether they contain older Linux/Chromium code. It reports no check of whether VentiVul functions appear in the DL training sets or in LLM pretraining corpora (pp. 3–4).
91	- Conflict of interest: [I] ICVul, one of the four training benchmarks, is the authors' own dataset (Lu, Li, Dehaene, Lagaisse, MSR 2025; p. 3, reference list p. 18). The paper presents it as "high-quality" (p. 3). Its results are not singled out favourably, but the dependence should be noted. Funding: not reported (no funding or acknowledgement statement in the text).
92	- External: [I] C/C++, two very large projects, 200 CVEs, open-weight mid-size LLMs only (p. 4, p. 5).
93	- Construct: [I] Labelling unrelated same-file functions as non-vulnerable (p. 4) is a realistic construct for "scan the whole file", though label noise remains (p. 17). PACC is a strict and useful measure of patch sensitivity. CDR rewards indiscriminate positive prediction, as the paper itself shows (p. 13).
94	- Statistical conclusion: [I] No tests, single runs, small per-CWE cells (p. 14).
95	- Reproducibility: [I] Good overall: data, code and results are public (p. 2), and the decoding settings are fully given (p. 8). Prompt templates are given (Table 4, p. 9), but the system prompt is only paraphrased (p. 8) and the few-shot demonstrations are not listed in the paper. DL hyper-parameters are given only by reference to the original implementations (p. 8), and DL run counts and seeds are not reported.
96	
97	## 11. Future research directions
98	- Stated by authors [A]: representations and training that emphasise security-relevant changes, e.g. vulnerable–patched pair supervision (p. 16); datasets prioritising reliable labels, diverse patterns and explicit vulnerability–fix links over size (p. 16); complementing within-dataset evaluation with cross-dataset and temporally separated testing, and reporting CDR and patch-pair metrics with function-level metrics (p. 16); studying individual dataset factors, broader ecosystems and "more advanced LLM adaptation strategies" (p. 16).
99	- Suggested by us [I]: run SAST tools and frontier/fine-tuned LLMs on VentiVul with file/repository context and a chance baseline. That would give exactly the same-benchmark LLM vs SAST vs DL comparison our RQ5 identifies as missing.
100	
101	## 12. Relevance to our research
102	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (DL vs LLM on largely shared OOD data), RQ2 (temporal separation, cross-dataset shift, class ratio, accuracy vs F1), RQ4 (per-project and per-CWE variation, C/C++), RQ5 (patch-pair sensitivity, chance baselines).
103	- How it informs our work [I]: This is direct, peer-reviewed (JSS 2026) evidence that in-distribution DL scores do not survive temporal shift. It is consistent with ding2025vulnerability, which shows BigVul-trained models collapse on PrimeVul [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7]. LineVul's F1 falls from 91–94.5 in-distribution (p. 12) to 4.39–6.87 on VentiVul, and all 8 DL configurations score 3.47–8.65 (p. 13). On F1, the evaluated open-weight LLMs (≤ 32B) do no better than the shifted DL detectors (0.79–5.36), and both families sit within a few points of the all-positive F1 of ≈ 3.87%. On PACC, both families are far below the random q(1−q) level (up to 25%), i.e. they rarely tell a function apart from its patch. It supports the RQ2 claim that evaluation setup drives the reported ranking. It covers no SAST tool or cost, so it adds nothing for RQ3.

28	## 1. Research objective
29	[A] To test whether high accuracies reported for learning-based detectors on synthetic corpora and random splits (including the authors' own SentinelCMS, ~93% accuracy on 600 synthetic snippets) transfer to real, disclosed WordPress plugin vulnerabilities. The second aim is to quantify how much duplicate leakage, contradictory labels and in-sample stacking inflated the authors' own first release (p. 2). The paper is a self-correcting re-evaluation prompted by an audit of the first release (p. 2; acknowledgment p. 14).
30	
31	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
32	- [A] RQ1 (transfer): does training on real CVE data beat training on synthetic data? (p. 2)
33	- [A] RQ2 (detector families): how do static, classical and neural detectors compare under duplicate-controlled evaluation? (p. 2)
34	- [A] RQ3 (negatives and granularity): how do the negative-sampling variant and label granularity affect results? (p. 2)
35	- [A] RQ4 (evaluation validity): how much do duplicate leakage and in-sample stacking inflate reported performance? (p. 2)
36	- No formal hypotheses are stated.

38	## 3. Methodology
39	- Research design: [V] Benchmark construction plus a comparative evaluation of ten detector configurations under plugin-grouped five-fold cross-validation on complete held-out folds (p. 1, p. 5–6).
40	- Approach / model / intervention:
41	  - [V] **Static analysis (SAST arm):** a "two-pass intra-procedural analyzer" that propagates taint from user-controlled sources to security-sensitive sinks without sanitisation (p. 5). It is **not named and no version is given** (p. 5). The authors call it "intra-procedural and lexical" (p. 13).
42	  - [I] From the description alone it does not match an established PHP SAST tool (e.g. Pixy, RIPS, Psalm/Phan taint mode, Semgrep), and it is most likely the taint component of the authors' own SentinelCMS (p. 2). The paper says neither; this rests on the missing name/version (p. 5) and the SentinelCMS description (p. 2).
43	  - [V] **Classical ML:** Random Forest and linear SVM on character 2–4-gram TF-IDF (char_wb, max_features 5000) (p. 5–6).
44	  - [V] **Neural:** Bi-LSTM with attention, a unidirectional LSTM ablation, and a "combined" model that concatenates the taint verdict to the Bi-LSTM representation (p. 5).
45	  - [V] **Stacking:** logistic-regression meta-learner, in an in-sample form (the original buggy implementation, kept only to measure bias) and a nested out-of-fold form (the citable one). The LSTM tower is omitted from both (p. 5–6).
46	  - [V] **No LLMs and no pre-trained transformers were run.** CodeBERT was not run "because the transformers library is not installed in the evaluation environment and the host has no GPU" (p. 13). LLMs appear only in related work (p. 3).
47	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] Three deliberately trivial baselines (p. 5):
48	  - majority class (always predicts the most frequent training class);
49	  - a source/sink presence rule (the same rule used for label cleaning);
50	  - a one-feature logistic regression on function token count.
51	  - [V] RQ1 also compares a Bi-LSTM trained on the 600-snippet synthetic corpus with real-to-real CV (p. 7).
52	
53	## 4. Dataset and sample
54	- Data source(s): [V] NVD CVE API v2 and CVEProject/cvelistV5. 6666 unique indexed CVE records; 1757 CVEs in 1281 plugins could be resolved to downloadable pre-fix/post-fix source pairs (p. 3). About 54% of indexed CVEs were unrecoverable because old releases/SVN tags were pruned (p. 3).
55	- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] PHP functions. 30,860 snippets per variant before de-duplication; 15,294 (Variant A) and 24,917 (Variant B) after leakage control (p. 5, Table 2).
56	  - **Class balance / prevalence:**
57	    - [V] Variant A: Safe/XSS/SQLi/RCE = 3895/8446/2104/849 (p. 5, Table 2), so vulnerable is the majority class; the majority baseline accuracy is 0.745 (p. 9).
58	    - [V] Variant B: 13,396/8531/2142/848 (p. 5, Table 2); majority baseline accuracy 0.538 (p. 8, Table 6).
59	    - [I] Vulnerable prevalence is therefore 74.5% (A) and 46.2% (B) (our calculation from Table 2 counts). Both are far above realistic prevalence because negatives come only from vulnerable plugins: the patched twins of vulnerable functions in Variant A, untouched functions of the same plugin in Variant B (p. 3).
60	  - [V] Test folds are complete and prevalence-preserving; no balancing or subsampling of test folds (p. 6).
61	- Sampling / selection method: [V] Labels come from tree-sitter diffs of vulnerable vs patched versions (p. 3):
62	  - functions touched by the fix are positives and receive the CVE's vulnerability type; untouched functions are negatives;
63	  - Variant A uses the patched twin as the negative; Variant B uses unmodified functions from the same plugin.
64	- Leakage control: [V] An audit of the first release found (p. 4, Table 1):
65	  - duplicate groups crossing folds: 166 groups / 1086 records (A) and 151 / 676 (B);
66	  - contradictory-label groups: 730 / 456 (1852 / 1199 records).
67	  - [V] Three corrections were applied (p. 4):
68	    - all conflicting-label hash groups were removed;
69	    - exact duplicates (SHA-256 of whitespace-normalised code) were merged;
70	    - near-duplicates were grouped into clone families (MinHash over 5-token shingles, Jaccard ≥ 0.9; AST node-type sequences, Jaccard ≥ 0.9) and each family was collapsed to one record.
71	  - [V] Grouping by connected components was rejected because one giant component covered 59.4% (A) / 72.1% (B) of the corpus (p. 4).
72	  - [V] Final folds share 0 hashes, 0 clone families and 0 plugins (p. 5, Table 2).
73	  - [V] All three corrections together reduced the published 30,860 records by 50.4% (A) and 19.3% (B). Clone-family collapse alone removed 11,123 (A) and 3714 (B) records; conflict removal plus exact deduplication left 26,417 / 28,631 before that step (p. 5, Table 2).
74	  - [V] There is no temporal split; all CVEs predate the experiments and no date cut-off is applied (pp. 3–6). [I] Temporal leakage is not addressed; it is less relevant here because no pre-trained model is used.
75	- Label quality: [V] A stratified 400-function expert review (single annotator, blind to the automated verdict) found (p. 11, Table 10):
76	  - HIGH tier precision 73.0% (27/37);
77	  - MEDIUM tier 44.7% (97/217);
78	  - LOW (discarded) tier 0.7% (1/146);
79	  - cleaned subset (HIGH+MEDIUM) 48.8% (124/254).
80	- Data availability (public? link?): [V] Labels, metadata, hashes, folds and a loader script are on GitHub (Aisultan05/wordpress-cve-benchmark) and Zenodo; the audited rebuild is release v2.1.0. Plugin source is not redistributed but reconstructed from WordPress.org (p. 14). [V] A 125-vulnerability / 247-safe expert-verified subset is released (p. 11).

82	## 5. Experimental setup
83	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools:
84	  - [V] Splits and losses: StratifiedGroupKFold (scikit-learn 1.8.0), 5 folds, seed 42, grouped by plugin slug; class-weighted cross-entropy (p. 6, Table 3).
85	  - [V] LSTM settings (p. 6, Table 3):
86	    - sequence length 128, 40 epochs, embedding 64, hidden 128, 2 layers, dropout 0.3, batch 16, Adam lr 1e-3;
87	    - at most 4000 training records per fold; CPU only.
88	  - [V] RF: 300 trees, balanced class weights. LinearSVC: C 1.0, balanced (p. 6).
89	  - [V] Software: Python 3.14, PyTorch 2.11 (CPU), NumPy 2.4, tree-sitter-php (p. 7).
90	  - [V] The 128-token bound was chosen for tractability, not tuned; its effect is unmeasured (p. 6).
91	  - [V] Granularities: binary, three-class (Safe/SQLi/XSS) and four-class (+RCE), crossed with the two variants, giving six settings (p. 6).
92	  - [V] Result files are keyed to SHA-256 fingerprints of the dataset index and fold file (p. 6).
93	- Code availability: [V] Data, folds, per-fold predictions, scores and fingerprinted results are released (p. 1, p. 14). [I] Whether training code is in the same repository is implied ("released training scripts", p. 6) but the repository was not inspected.

95	## 6. Evaluation metrics
96	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
97	  - [V] Macro-F1 is the headline metric (fold mean ± SD, 95% CI with t, 4 df) (p. 6).
98	  - [V] Also reported: accuracy, per-class precision/recall/F1, vulnerable-class recall and FNR, balanced accuracy, MCC and PR-AUC (p. 6).
99	  - [A] Accuracy is not comparable with the earlier release because collapsing changed the majority class; macro-F1, balanced accuracy and MCC should be used instead (p. 5, Table 2 note).
100	  - [V] **Vulnerable-class F1 alone is not reported for most models** (only per-class F1 for the Variant B four-class setting, p. 9, Table 7). [I] Headline numbers are therefore not directly comparable with the vulnerable-class F1 used by most studies in our corpus.
101	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals):
102	  - [V] Paired tests across folds and across plugins, with Cohen's d; the plugin-level test is "the better-powered" (p. 6).
103	  - [V] Only one comparison is reported in the text: RF vs majority on Variant A macro-F1 is "significant across folds but not across plugins (Wilcoxon p = 0.295, Cohen's d = 0.057)" (p. 9). The only quantified result is the plugin-level one (p = 0.295, d = 0.057); the fold-level test is not named and its p-value is not reported (p. 6, p. 9).
104	  - [I] With only five paired fold observations (p. 6), a two-sided exact Wilcoxon signed-rank test cannot reach p < 0.05 (smallest attainable p = 2/32 = 0.0625), so the fold-level "significant" result must come from a different test (e.g. a paired t-test) or a one-sided test. Basis: standard property of the exact Wilcoxon test at n = 5.
105	  - [V] 95% CIs are reported for Variant B binary (p. 8, Table 6).
106	  - [V] No multiple-comparison correction is mentioned (pp. 6–9).

136	    - Variant B binary (46.2% vulnerable): an always-vulnerable predictor would score vulnerable-class F1 ≈ 0.632 and macro-F1 ≈ 0.316. The reported majority (always-Safe) baseline is 0.350 (p. 8).
137	    - Variant A binary (74.5% vulnerable): the majority baseline *is* always-vulnerable, at macro-F1 0.427 (p. 8, Table 5).

143	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
144	- [A] The protocol is "duplicate-controlled rather than provably leakage-free"; semantic clones that differ lexically and structurally may persist (p. 13).
145	- [A] About 54% of indexed CVEs were unrecoverable, so the corpus may be biased toward plugins that retain historical versions (p. 13).
146	- [A] Rare-class estimates are unreliable (RCE 848 records in Variant B; several models never predict it); four-class results are indicative only (p. 13).
147	- [A] Neural models trained on ≤4000 records/fold for 40 epochs on CPU, so their numbers are a lower bound (p. 13).
148	- [A] No transformer comparison (CodeBERT not run; no GPU); the 256-token sensitivity run is outstanding (p. 13).
149	- [A] The taint analyser is intra-procedural and lexical (p. 13).
150	- [A] Labels are only about half correct on the positive class, which "bounds what any model trained on them can demonstrate" (p. 13).
151	- [A] The expert sample was labelled by a single annotator, so no inter-annotator agreement is reported (p. 11).
152	
153	## 9. Limitations we identified
154	- [I] **The SAST arm is a weak straw-man for our RQ1.** It is an unnamed in-house intra-procedural lexical analyser (p. 5, p. 13). No established PHP SAST tool (e.g. Psalm taint analysis, Semgrep, RIPS/Pixy descendants) was run. (That CodeQL does not support PHP is our outside knowledge, not stated in the paper.) The "misses about 98%" result cannot be generalised to PHP SAST.
155	- [I] **No LLM arm at all** (p. 3, p. 13). For our review the paper informs SAST-vs-DL and evaluation methodology, not LLM-vs-anything.
156	- [I] **Label precision of the main benchmark is not reported.** The 48.8% figure (p. 11) refers to the cleaned HIGH+MEDIUM subset. The main experiments (Tables 5–6) use the full corpus, which also contains LOW-tier functions found 0.7% genuine (p. 11) and the 13,702 "noisy" discarded pairs (p. 11, Table 11). Genuine-positive precision in the evaluated corpus is therefore plausibly well below 48.8%, but is not reported. This makes every absolute score hard to interpret.
157	- [I] **Macro-F1 headline** mixes Safe-class and vulnerable-class F1. Combined with class proportions that differ between variants (74.5% vs 46.2% vulnerable), this makes cross-variant and cross-paper comparisons fragile.
158	- [I] **Function-level granularity, not repository-level.** It does not test inter-procedural or cross-file detection, which is the core of our G5 interest. The inter-procedural recovery experiment found only 39 paths (p. 11).
159	- [I] **Self-correction context.** The paper corrects the authors' own earlier release after reviewers audited the artifacts (p. 2, p. 14). This is commendable transparency, but it also means the earlier SentinelCMS numbers (~93%, p. 2) should not be cited.
160	- [I] **Minor presentation issues:**
161	  - The statements are in the singular ("The author declares", "The author thanks") for a six-author paper (p. 14).
162	  - Only one comparison is tested in the text, with only the plugin-level p-value given, despite paired tests being described for model comparisons (p. 6, p. 9; see §6).
163	- [I] **No negatives from unrelated code at realistic prevalence.** Both variants draw negatives from vulnerable plugins only, so the deployment false-alarm rate is unknown.
164	
165	## 10. Threats to validity
166	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection):
167	  - [V] Strong exact- and near-duplicate control with verified 0/0/0 cross-fold overlap (p. 5).
168	  - [V] In-sample stacking leakage is measured and corrected (p. 10).
169	  - [A] Semantic clones may remain (p. 13).
170	  - [I] Label noise (≤48.8% genuine positives) is the dominant confound. Diff-based labelling marks every function touched by a fix as vulnerable, including non-security edits (p. 4, p. 11).
171	  - [V] The filtered-subset comparison is confounded by easier test cases (p. 10).
172	- External (generalisability of sample/context):
173	  - [V] WordPress plugins only, PHP only, XSS/SQLi/RCE only (p. 5).
174	  - [A] Survivorship bias toward plugins with retained history (p. 13).
175	  - [I] Results may not transfer to other PHP frameworks (Laravel, Drupal) or to repository-level detection.
176	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?):
177	  - [I] Macro-F1 averages a Safe-class F1 that depends heavily on negative sampling (Variant A vs B).
178	  - [I] Labels measure "touched by a security fix" more than "vulnerable".
179	  - [V] The per-class tables expose degenerate predictors that aggregate scores hide (p. 9).
180	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance):
181	  - [V] 5 folds give only five paired observations; a plugin-level test is used as the better-powered alternative (p. 6).
182	  - [V] CIs are reported for Variant B binary only (p. 8).
183	  - [V] No multiple-comparison correction is reported (pp. 6–10).
184	  - [V] A single seed (42) is used throughout (p. 7).
185	  - [I] Many between-model gaps (e.g. 0.562–0.601 on Variant B binary) have overlapping CIs (p. 8, Table 6).
186	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Good — hyper-parameters (p. 6–7), folds, per-fold predictions, fingerprinted results and a loader script are released (p. 14). Plugin code must be re-downloaded from WordPress.org (p. 14). [I] Reproducibility therefore depends on WordPress.org continuing to host old versions, the same pruning that already lost 54% of CVEs (p. 3).
187	- Funding and conflicts of interest: [V] "This research received no external funding"; no conflicts of interest are declared (p. 14). [I] The study re-evaluates the authors' own SentinelCMS (p. 2), so it is a self-evaluation; however, any bias would run against the authors' own earlier claims (~93% accuracy, p. 2), which the paper largely retracts, so it is unlikely to inflate the reported results.

200	## 12. Relevance to our research
201	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ2 (primary), RQ1 (SAST vs ML/DL only; no LLM), RQ4 (PHP; per-CWE-class behaviour), RQ5.
202	- How it informs our work [I]:
203	  - **RQ2:** a clean demonstration that duplicate leakage, contradictory labels, in-sample stacking and label noise shape measured performance more than model family. It is also a second study (beside shu2026evaluating) that reports trivial baselines and finds they are competitive, which strengthens G1.
204	  - **G5 (PHP):** gives real-CVE PHP evidence, but at function level and without LLMs or a standard SAST tool. The released corpus and expert-verified subset are a ready data source for a G5 study. G5 stays open only pending a novelty check against a likely competitor: Neef et al. 2026 (arXiv:2606.21397, "Evaluating LLMs for Real-World Web Vulnerability Detection"), which deininger2026open cites as comparing models on "web vulnerability detection in WordPress plugins" [@deininger2026open, p. 3]. It is not in our corpus and was not read; its content is unknown beyond that citation.
205	  - **G2:** the closest PHP analogue to a leakage-controlled same-benchmark comparison, missing the LLM arm.
206	  - **RQ4:** XSS is detected far better than RCE by learned models (p. 9), and SQLi per-class F1 is ≤ 0.146 (p. 9, Table 7). This is a hint that rare classes are effectively undetected by small ML models on PHP.
207	  - **C5 (class balance):** the choice of negatives flips the majority class and the failure direction of the same RF model (p. 9).

21	- Year / venue: 2026, Computers and Artificial Intelligence (published) — **venue flag [I]:** published by Zeus Press (p. 1); no peer-review statement or received/accepted dates in the PDF (pp. 1–16); low-visibility source not in DOAJ (OpenAlex, 2026-11-12). 28	## 1. Research objective
29	- [A] Review source-code vulnerability detection with "lightweight code Transformers and large-scale language models" as the two lines of discussion, covering input construction, task adaptation, use of program-analysis information and multi-model collaboration, and compare them by datasets, metrics and deployment conditions (p. 1).
30	- [A] Scope is limited to source-code-level detection, localization and classification; network intrusion, malware, smart contracts, vulnerability generation and automatic repair are excluded (p. 1).
31	
32	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
33	- [A] Three organising questions in the introduction: what capabilities methods actually improve, under what data conditions/protocols the gains are obtained, and whether evidence suffices for real-world deployment (p. 2).
34	- [A] Four formal RQs: RQ1 development from sequence/graph models to code pretraining and LLM interaction; RQ2 performance evidence of direct prompting, in-context learning, fine-tuning, structural enhancement and multi-model collaboration; RQ3 effects of label noise, duplication, class imbalance and temporal leakage; RQ4 how cross-project, out-of-time, false-positive-cost, localization and explanation evaluation approach deployment (p. 4).
35	- [I] The two framings are not reconciled: the introduction organises the paper around "three closely related questions" (p. 2), while Section 3.1 sets four formal RQs (p. 4), and the paper does not map one onto the other. Separately, it gives "medium confidence to C2" (p. 12), but no claim labelled C1/C2 is defined anywhere in the text.

37	## 3. Methodology
38	- Research design: [I] Narrative (traditional) review. The paper calls itself a "review" (p. 1) and gives no search strategy, databases, search strings, date window, inclusion/exclusion screening, PRISMA flow, or study-quality assessment — all "not reported". The only inclusion rule stated is that it "includes only studies that directly analyze source code" and excludes repair (p. 4).
39	- Approach / taxonomy: [A] Methods are classified "by how vulnerability knowledge is acquired" rather than by model scale, core technology or supply-chain stage as in earlier reviews (p. 4). Two routes: (a) lightweight code Transformers — code pretraining + supervised fine-tuning, input granularity, structural fusion (pp. 5–6); (b) large-scale LLMs — supervised fine-tuning/steering, multitask learning, direct prompting, few-shot/ICL, hybrid detection with program analysis, ensembles/multi-model collaboration, explanation (pp. 6–9). Figure 1 adds cross-cutting layers "Data and bias", "Reliability evaluation" and "Discussion and outlook" (p. 3) [V, from figure].
40	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [A] Traditional methods (SAST, GNNs) are discussed "only in two situations": to motivate structural information for Transformers and as baselines or external tools for LLMs; "this paper does not provide a separate review of traditional detection methods" (p. 4). Section 7.1 nevertheless compares LLMs with DL and SAST qualitatively (pp. 11–12).

Several references are themselves reviews/surveys [2–4, 18–21] (pp. 14–15).

49	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: not applicable (no experiments). 53	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: [A] The review recommends reporting at least Precision, Recall, F1 and a confusion matrix, grouped by project, time, language or CWE; Top-k and audit effort at fixed recall for localization; separate checks of location/type/cause/suggestion for explanations; Accuracy only as supplementary; mean, fluctuation range and parse-failure rate for repeated LLM calls (p. 11).
