56	## 7. Key findings
57	1. Benchmark inflation — [A] Gains from code pretraining, prompting, fine-tuning and structural enhancement hold "on specific benchmarks" but are "easily affected by duplicate samples, label noise, random splits, temporal leakage, and changes in model versions" (p. 1). Supported by the PrimeVul re-report (primary source: [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7]): StarCoder2 F1 68.26% on BigVul vs 3.09% on the PrimeVul test set (p. 2) and the five-model ranges above (p. 12).
58	2. Random-split F1 should be called "within-benchmark performance", not a real-world detection rate; out-of-time testing should be a reliability baseline, combined with project isolation and reporting of time windows, data-freeze dates and model knowledge cutoffs (p. 10) — [A].
59	3. Contamination from pretraining corpora is treated "as an alternative explanation that needs to be audited", not a confirmed fact; knowledge-cutoff dates are not proof of no contamination (p. 10) — [A].
60	4. Cross-study ranking is not possible: GRACE, DLAP, context enhancement and M2CVD "all report gains in their own settings, but datasets, model versions, and evaluation protocols differ, so they cannot be directly ranked" (p. 12) — [A]. [A] Table 2 is a normative risk matrix (the author's recommendations, not data): label noise, exact/near duplicates, pretraining contamination, random splitting, cross-project/language failure, class imbalance, false-positive cost, explanation/version validity, each with identification signals and mitigations (pp. 10–11).
61	5. LLM vs SAST vs DL — [A] "SAST is usually more stable within the scope covered by existing rules, whereas LLMs are better at semantic summarization and alert explanation"; unified benchmarks "support complementarity rather than complete replacement", with the two tool types finding different vulnerabilities and different false positives (p. 12). It cites [1] and [15]. [1] is a SAST-only study of query-based C/C++ tools (p. 14); [15] is the Gnieciak & Szandala LLM-vs-SAST benchmark (p. 15), its only head-to-head source. No numbers for this comparison are given. [I] Qin leaves out that [15] found LLMs above SAST on mean F1 (0.75–0.80 vs 0.26–0.55) [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10]. "SAST is usually more stable" is therefore not supported by its own cited comparison. Cite gnieciak2025large directly for this comparison.
62	6. Hybrids — [A] Proposed workflow: "SAST candidate generation-LLM review or explanation-human confirmation" (p. 8), to be judged by audit time, false-negative control and explanation consistency rather than overall F1 (p. 8); outputs should not be "simply concatenate[d]" (p. 13). Evidence cited is GRACE (structure + ICL, ≥28.65% relative F1 gain over six baselines, p. 8), DLAP (DL-augmented prompting, p. 8) and the context-enhancement study [29] (p. 8). No quantitative evidence on SAST+LLM hybrids is reported.
63	7. Cost — [A] API calls, GPU memory, latency, model updates and prompt maintenance should be counted; sensitive code and local large-scale scanning suit lightweight models or SAST; high-risk scenarios should use hybrid workflows with human confirmation (p. 12). No cost figures are reported.
64	8. Re-reported primary numbers (all [A], from cited papers): LineVul 188k+ functions, F1 +160%–379% over baselines, Top-10 Accuracy +12%–25%, Effort@20%Recall −29%–53% (p. 5); DiverseVul 7,514 commits, 18,945 vulnerable / 330,492 non-vulnerable functions, 150 CWEs (p. 9); LLMVulExp average F1 92.4% on SeVC single-type setting (p. 8).

18	# A Real CVE-Backed Benchmark for WordPress Plugin Vulnerability Detection: Re-Evaluating Static and Learning-Based Detectors Under Leakage-Controlled Evaluation
19	
20	- Authors: Tashenova, Zhuldyz; Aitmagambetuly, Aisultan; Urynbassarova, Altyn; Zhetkerbay, Askhat; Amanzholova, Shirin; Kerim, Akerke
21	- Year / venue: 2026, Big Data and Cognitive Computing (published)
22	- DOI: 10.3390/bdcc10090303 · URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/bdcc10090303
23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
24	
25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
26	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
27	
28	## 1. Research objective
29	[A] To test whether high accuracies reported for learning-based detectors on synthetic corpora and random splits (including the authors' own SentinelCMS, ~93% accuracy on 600 synthetic snippets) transfer to real, disclosed WordPress plugin vulnerabilities. The second aim is to quantify how much duplicate leakage, contradictory labels and in-sample stacking inflated the authors' own first release (p. 2). The paper is a self-correcting re-evaluation prompted by an audit of the first release (p. 2; acknowledgment p. 14).
30	
31	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
32	- [A] RQ1 (transfer): does training on real CVE data beat training on synthetic data? (p. 2)
33	- [A] RQ2 (detector families): how do static, classical and neural detectors compare under duplicate-controlled evaluation? (p. 2)
34	- [A] RQ3 (negatives and granularity): how do the negative-sampling variant and label granularity affect results? (p. 2)
35	- [A] RQ4 (evaluation validity): how much do duplicate leakage and in-sample stacking inflate reported performance? (p. 2)
36	- No formal hypotheses are stated.
37	
38	## 3. Methodology
39	- Research design: [V] Benchmark construction plus a comparative evaluation of ten detector configurations under plugin-grouped five-fold cross-validation on complete held-out folds (p. 1, p. 5–6).
40	- Approach / model / intervention:
41	  - [V] **Static analysis (SAST arm):** a "two-pass intra-procedural analyzer" that propagates taint from user-controlled sources to security-sensitive sinks without sanitisation (p. 5). It is **not named and no version is given** (p. 5). The authors call it "intra-procedural and lexical" (p. 13).
42	  - [I] From the description alone it does not match an established PHP SAST tool (e.g. Pixy, RIPS, Psalm/Phan taint mode, Semgrep), and it is most likely the taint component of the authors' own SentinelCMS (p. 2). The paper says neither; this rests on the missing name/version (p. 5) and the SentinelCMS description (p. 2).
43	  - [V] **Classical ML:** Random Forest and linear SVM on character 2–4-gram TF-IDF (char_wb, max_features 5000) (p. 5–6).
44	  - [V] **Neural:** Bi-LSTM with attention, a unidirectional LSTM ablation, and a "combined" model that concatenates the taint verdict to the Bi-LSTM representation (p. 5).
45	  - [V] **Stacking:** logistic-regression meta-learner, in an in-sample form (the original buggy implementation, kept only to measure bias) and a nested out-of-fold form (the citable one). The LSTM tower is omitted from both (p. 5–6).
46	  - [V] **No LLMs and no pre-trained transformers were run.** CodeBERT was not run "because the transformers library is not installed in the evaluation environment and the host has no GPU" (p. 13). LLMs appear only in related work (p. 3).
47	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] Three deliberately trivial baselines (p. 5):
48	  - majority class (always predicts the most frequent training class);
49	  - a source/sink presence rule (the same rule used for label cleaning);
50	  - a one-feature logistic regression on function token count.
51	  - [V] RQ1 also compares a Bi-LSTM trained on the 600-snippet synthetic corpus with real-to-real CV (p. 7).
52	
53	## 4. Dataset and sample
54	- Data source(s): [V] NVD CVE API v2 and CVEProject/cvelistV5. 6666 unique indexed CVE records; 1757 CVEs in 1281 plugins could be resolved to downloadable pre-fix/post-fix source pairs (p. 3). About 54% of indexed CVEs were unrecoverable because old releases/SVN tags were pruned (p. 3).
55	- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] PHP functions. 30,860 snippets per variant before de-duplication; 15,294 (Variant A) and 24,917 (Variant B) after leakage control (p. 5, Table 2).
56	  - **Class balance / prevalence:**
57	    - [V] Variant A: Safe/XSS/SQLi/RCE = 3895/8446/2104/849 (p. 5, Table 2), so vulnerable is the majority class; the majority baseline accuracy is 0.745 (p. 9).
58	    - [V] Variant B: 13,396/8531/2142/848 (p. 5, Table 2); majority baseline accuracy 0.538 (p. 8, Table 6).
59	    - [I] Vulnerable prevalence is therefore 74.5% (A) and 46.2% (B) (our calculation from Table 2 counts). Both are far above realistic prevalence because negatives come only from vulnerable plugins: the patched twins of vulnerable functions in Variant A, untouched functions of the same plugin in Variant B (p. 3).
60	  - [V] Test folds are complete and prevalence-preserving; no balancing or subsampling of test folds (p. 6).
61	- Sampling / selection method: [V] Labels come from tree-sitter diffs of vulnerable vs patched versions (p. 3):
62	  - functions touched by the fix are positives and receive the CVE's vulnerability type; untouched functions are negatives;
63	  - Variant A uses the patched twin as the negative; Variant B uses unmodified functions from the same plugin.
64	- Leakage control: [V] An audit of the first release found (p. 4, Table 1):
65	  - duplicate groups crossing folds: 166 groups / 1086 records (A) and 151 / 676 (B);
66	  - contradictory-label groups: 730 / 456 (1852 / 1199 records).
67	  - [V] Three corrections were applied (p. 4):
68	    - all conflicting-label hash groups were removed;
69	    - exact duplicates (SHA-256 of whitespace-normalised code) were merged;
70	    - near-duplicates were grouped into clone families (MinHash over 5-token shingles, Jaccard ≥ 0.9; AST node-type sequences, Jaccard ≥ 0.9) and each family was collapsed to one record.
71	  - [V] Grouping by connected components was rejected because one giant component covered 59.4% (A) / 72.1% (B) of the corpus (p. 4).
72	  - [V] Final folds share 0 hashes, 0 clone families and 0 plugins (p. 5, Table 2).
73	  - [V] All three corrections together reduced the published 30,860 records by 50.4% (A) and 19.3% (B). Clone-family collapse alone removed 11,123 (A) and 3714 (B) records; conflict removal plus exact deduplication left 26,417 / 28,631 before that step (p. 5, Table 2).
74	  - [V] There is no temporal split; all CVEs predate the experiments and no date cut-off is applied (pp. 3–6). [I] Temporal leakage is not addressed; it is less relevant here because no pre-trained model is used.
75	- Label quality: [V] A stratified 400-function expert review (single annotator, blind to the automated verdict) found (p. 11, Table 10):
76	  - HIGH tier precision 73.0% (27/37);
77	  - MEDIUM tier 44.7% (97/217);
78	  - LOW (discarded) tier 0.7% (1/146);
79	  - cleaned subset (HIGH+MEDIUM) 48.8% (124/254).
80	- Data availability (public? link?): [V] Labels, metadata, hashes, folds and a loader script are on GitHub (Aisultan05/wordpress-cve-benchmark) and Zenodo; the audited rebuild is release v2.1.0. Plugin source is not redistributed but reconstructed from WordPress.org (p. 14). [V] A 125-vulnerability / 247-safe expert-verified subset is released (p. 11).

82	## 5. Experimental setup
83	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools:
84	  - [V] Splits and losses: StratifiedGroupKFold (scikit-learn 1.8.0), 5 folds, seed 42, grouped by plugin slug; class-weighted cross-entropy (p. 6, Table 3).
85	  - [V] LSTM settings (p. 6, Table 3):
86	    - sequence length 128, 40 epochs, embedding 64, hidden 128, 2 layers, dropout 0.3, batch 16, Adam lr 1e-3;
87	    - at most 4000 training records per fold; CPU only.
88	  - [V] RF: 300 trees, balanced class weights. LinearSVC: C 1.0, balanced (p. 6).
89	  - [V] Software: Python 3.14, PyTorch 2.11 (CPU), NumPy 2.4, tree-sitter-php (p. 7).
90	  - [V] The 128-token bound was chosen for tractability, not tuned; its effect is unmeasured (p. 6).
91	  - [V] Granularities: binary, three-class (Safe/SQLi/XSS) and four-class (+RCE), crossed with the two variants, giving six settings (p. 6).
92	  - [V] Result files are keyed to SHA-256 fingerprints of the dataset index and fold file (p. 6).
93	- Code availability: [V] Data, folds, per-fold predictions, scores and fingerprinted results are released (p. 1, p. 14). [I] Whether training code is in the same repository is implied ("released training scripts", p. 6) but the repository was not inspected.

95	## 6. Evaluation metrics
96	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
97	  - [V] Macro-F1 is the headline metric (fold mean ± SD, 95% CI with t, 4 df) (p. 6).
98	  - [V] Also reported: accuracy, per-class precision/recall/F1, vulnerable-class recall and FNR, balanced accuracy, MCC and PR-AUC (p. 6).
99	  - [A] Accuracy is not comparable with the earlier release because collapsing changed the majority class; macro-F1, balanced accuracy and MCC should be used instead (p. 5, Table 2 note).
100	  - [V] **Vulnerable-class F1 alone is not reported for most models** (only per-class F1 for the Variant B four-class setting, p. 9, Table 7). [I] Headline numbers are therefore not directly comparable with the vulnerable-class F1 used by most studies in our corpus.
101	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals):
102	  - [V] Paired tests across folds and across plugins, with Cohen's d; the plugin-level test is "the better-powered" (p. 6).
103	  - [V] Only one comparison is reported in the text: RF vs majority on Variant A macro-F1 is "significant across folds but not across plugins (Wilcoxon p = 0.295, Cohen's d = 0.057)" (p. 9). The only quantified result is the plugin-level one (p = 0.295, d = 0.057); the fold-level test is not named and its p-value is not reported (p. 6, p. 9).
104	  - [I] With only five paired fold observations (p. 6), a two-sided exact Wilcoxon signed-rank test cannot reach p < 0.05 (smallest attainable p = 2/32 = 0.0625), so the fold-level "significant" result must come from a different test (e.g. a paired t-test) or a one-sided test. Basis: standard property of the exact Wilcoxon test at n = 5.
105	  - [V] 95% CIs are reported for Variant B binary (p. 8, Table 6).
106	  - [V] No multiple-comparison correction is mentioned (pp. 6–9).

[V] It detects 1.7–1.8% of vulnerabilities (p. 9); vulnerable FNR is 0.982 on Variant B binary (p. 8, Table 6). [V] On Variant A binary its macro-F1 (0.221) is below the majority baseline (0.427) (p. 8, Table 5). [A] The low recall "reflects that implementation rather than taint analysis in general" (p. 13).
128	4. **Trivial baselines are hard to beat** — [V] The token-count baseline matches or exceeds the TF-IDF RF in four of six settings (p. 8, Table 5). [A] The authors say it is "within one percentage point of the best neural model in Variant B binary (0.572 against 0.573)", i.e. the Bi-LSTM (p. 8). [V] In Table 5, however, the best neural model on Variant B binary is the uni-LSTM at 0.578, so the length baseline is 0.006 below the best neural model and 0.001 below the Bi-LSTM (p. 8, Table 5). [V] The Bi-LSTM's real-to-real Variant B binary macro-F1 is 0.572 in Table 4 but 0.573 in Table 5 (p. 7, p. 8). [V] The source/sink rule's MCC is −0.001 to 0.063 (p. 8). [A] "Much of what the models exploit is correlated with function size rather than with security-relevant structure" (p. 8).
129	5. **Degenerate predictors hidden by aggregate scores** — [V] On Variant A the RF labels 15,068 of 15,294 records vulnerable (Safe recall 0.032); its accuracy 0.747 exceeds the majority baseline's 0.745 by 0.15 pp (p. 9). [V] On Variant B the same RF has a vulnerable-class FNR of 0.84–0.87 (p. 9). [V] Several models almost never predict RCE: RF RCE F1 0.000, uni-LSTM 0.002 (p. 9, Table 7).
130	6. **Synthetic vs real training (RQ1)** — [V] Real-to-real Bi-LSTM beats synthetic-to-real only in binary settings (+0.034 and +0.078 macro-F1); in four-class settings synthetic is marginally ahead (−0.019, −0.017) (p. 7, Table 4).
131	7. **In-sample stacking bias (RQ4)** — [V] Mean +1.27 pp macro-F1; optimistic in 5 of 6 settings (max +2.95 pp) but −1.62 pp in Variant B binary (p. 10, Table 8). [A] Duplicate leakage is not expressed as a single number; the authors state that before correction "1086 and 676 records were exact copies of training material appearing in test folds" (p. 10). [V] Table 1 defines these numbers differently: 1086 (A) / 676 (B) are all records in the 166 / 151 duplicate groups that span more than one fold, which includes the training-side copies (p. 4, Table 1). [A] The filtered subset is easier as well as cleaner, so cleaning is "a plausible but unproven lever" (p. 10).

135	11. **Trivial-baseline comparison** — [I] Our calculation from Table 2 counts (p. 5):
136	    - Variant B binary (46.2% vulnerable): an always-vulnerable predictor would score vulnerable-class F1 ≈ 0.632 and macro-F1 ≈ 0.316. The reported majority (always-Safe) baseline is 0.350 (p. 8).
137	    - Variant A binary (74.5% vulnerable): the majority baseline *is* always-vulnerable, at macro-F1 0.427 (p. 8, Table 5).
138	    - Margins of the best detectors: Variant A, SVM 0.563 vs majority 0.427 = +0.136 (p. 8, Table 5); Variant B, nested stacking 0.601 vs majority 0.350 = +0.251, and vs our always-vulnerable 0.316 = +0.285 (p. 8, Table 6).

141	    - The 0.667 balanced-data reference does not apply, because neither variant is balanced and the metric is macro-F1.

143	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
144	- [A] The protocol is "duplicate-controlled rather than provably leakage-free"; semantic clones that differ lexically and structurally may persist (p. 13).
145	- [A] About 54% of indexed CVEs were unrecoverable, so the corpus may be biased toward plugins that retain historical versions (p. 13).
146	- [A] Rare-class estimates are unreliable (RCE 848 records in Variant B; several models never predict it); four-class results are indicative only (p. 13).
147	- [A] Neural models trained on ≤4000 records/fold for 40 epochs on CPU, so their numbers are a lower bound (p. 13).
148	- [A] No transformer comparison (CodeBERT not run; no GPU); the 256-token sensitivity run is outstanding (p. 13).
149	- [A] The taint analyser is intra-procedural and lexical (p. 13).
150	- [A] Labels are only about half correct on the positive class, which "bounds what any model trained on them can demonstrate" (p. 13).
151	- [A] The expert sample was labelled by a single annotator, so no inter-annotator agreement is reported (p. 11).
152	
153	## 9. Limitations we identified
154	- [I] **The SAST arm is a weak straw-man for our RQ1.** It is an unnamed in-house intra-procedural lexical analyser (p. 5, p. 13). No established PHP SAST tool (e.g. Psalm taint analysis, Semgrep, RIPS/Pixy descendants) was run. (That CodeQL does not support PHP is our outside knowledge, not stated in the paper.) The "misses about 98%" result cannot be generalised to PHP SAST.
155	- [I] **No LLM arm at all** (p. 3, p. 13). For our review the paper informs SAST-vs-DL and evaluation methodology, not LLM-vs-anything.
156	- [I] **Label precision of the main benchmark is not reported.** The 48.8% figure (p. 11) refers to the cleaned HIGH+MEDIUM subset. The main experiments (Tables 5–6) use the full corpus, which also contains LOW-tier functions found 0.7% genuine (p. 11) and the 13,702 "noisy" discarded pairs (p. 11, Table 11). Genuine-positive precision in the evaluated corpus is therefore plausibly well below 48.8%, but is not reported. This makes every absolute score hard to interpret.
157	- [I] **Macro-F1 headline** mixes Safe-class and vulnerable-class F1. Combined with class proportions that differ between variants (74.5% vs 46.2% vulnerable), this makes cross-variant and cross-paper comparisons fragile.
158	- [I] **Function-level granularity, not repository-level.** It does not test inter-procedural or cross-file detection, which is the core of our G5 interest. The inter-procedural recovery experiment found only 39 paths (p. 11).
159	- [I] **Self-correction context.** The paper corrects the authors' own earlier release after reviewers audited the artifacts (p. 2, p. 14). This is commendable transparency, but it also means the earlier SentinelCMS numbers (~93%, p. 2) should not be cited.
160	- [I] **Minor presentation issues:**
161	  - The statements are in the singular ("The author declares", "The author thanks") for a six-author paper (p. 14).
162	  - Only one comparison is tested in the text, with only the plugin-level p-value given, despite paired tests being described for model comparisons (p. 6, p. 9; see §6).
163	- [I] **No negatives from unrelated code at realistic prevalence.** Both variants draw negatives from vulnerable plugins only, so the deployment false-alarm rate is unknown.
164	
165	## 10. Threats to validity
166	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection):
167	  - [V] Strong exact- and near-duplicate control with verified 0/0/0 cross-fold overlap (p. 5).
168	  - [V] In-sample stacking leakage is measured and corrected (p. 10).
169	  - [A] Semantic clones may remain (p. 13).
170	  - [I] Label noise (≤48.8% genuine positives) is the dominant confound. Diff-based labelling marks every function touched by a fix as vulnerable, including non-security edits (p. 4, p. 11).
171	  - [V] The filtered-subset comparison is confounded by easier test cases (p. 10).
172	- External (generalisability of sample/context):
173	  - [V] WordPress plugins only, PHP only, XSS/SQLi/RCE only (p. 5).
174	  - [A] Survivorship bias toward plugins with retained history (p. 13).
175	  - [I] Results may not transfer to other PHP frameworks (Laravel, Drupal) or to repository-level detection.
176	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?):
177	  - [I] Macro-F1 averages a Safe-class F1 that depends heavily on negative sampling (Variant A vs B).
178	  - [I] Labels measure "touched by a security fix" more than "vulnerable".
179	  - [V] The per-class tables expose degenerate predictors that aggregate scores hide (p. 9).
180	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance):
181	  - [V] 5 folds give only five paired observations; a plugin-level test is used as the better-powered alternative (p. 6).
182	  - [V] CIs are reported for Variant B binary only (p. 8).
183	  - [V] No multiple-comparison correction is reported (pp. 6–10).
184	  - [V] A single seed (42) is used throughout (p. 7).
185	  - [I] Many between-model gaps (e.g. 0.562–0.601 on Variant B binary) have overlapping CIs (p. 8, Table 6).
186	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Good — hyper-parameters (p. 6–7), folds, per-fold predictions, fingerprinted results and a loader script are released (p. 14). Plugin code must be re-downloaded from WordPress.org (p. 14). [I] Reproducibility therefore depends on WordPress.org continuing to host old versions, the same pruning that already lost 54% of CVEs (p. 3).
187	- Funding and conflicts of interest: [V] "This research received no external funding"; no conflicts of interest are declared (p. 14). [I] The study re-evaluates the authors' own SentinelCMS (p. 2), so it is a self-evaluation; however, any bias would run against the authors' own earlier claims (~93% accuracy, p. 2), which the paper largely retracts, so it is unlikely to inflate the reported results.

189	## 11. Future research directions
190	- Stated by authors [A]:
191	  - extend expert review to several thousand functions with ≥2 annotators and adjudication, and evaluate on an expert-verified test set (p. 13);
192	  - use curated feeds that name entry points and sinks (p. 13);
193	  - semantic clone detection (p. 13);
194	  - a fully resourced transformer comparison on identical folds and a 256-token sensitivity run (p. 13);
195	  - require future detectors to clear trivial baselines such as function length (p. 13).
196	- Suggested by us [I]:
197	  - Run established PHP SAST tools (Semgrep PHP rules, Psalm taint mode, Progpilot) and 1–2 open LLMs on the released expert-verified 125/247 subset (p. 11). That would give a small but clean PHP LLM-vs-SAST-vs-ML comparison, directly addressing G5 and G2.
198	  - Report vulnerable-class F1 and precision at realistic prevalence alongside macro-F1.

200	## 12. Relevance to our research
201	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ2 (primary), RQ1 (SAST vs ML/DL only; no LLM), RQ4 (PHP; per-CWE-class behaviour), RQ5.
202	- How it informs our work [I]:
203	  - **RQ2:** a clean demonstration that duplicate leakage, contradictory labels, in-sample stacking and label noise shape measured performance more than model family. It is also a second study (beside shu2026evaluating) that reports trivial baselines and finds they are competitive, which strengthens G1.
204	  - **G5 (PHP):** gives real-CVE PHP evidence, but at function level and without LLMs or a standard SAST tool. The released corpus and expert-verified subset are a ready data source for a G5 study. G5 stays open only pending a novelty check against a likely competitor: Neef et al. 2026 (arXiv:2606.21397, "Evaluating LLMs for Real-World Web Vulnerability Detection"), which deininger2026open cites as comparing models on "web vulnerability detection in WordPress plugins" [@deininger2026open, p. 3]. It is not in our corpus and was not read; its content is unknown beyond that citation.
205	  - **G2:** the closest PHP analogue to a leakage-controlled same-benchmark comparison, missing the LLM arm.
206	  - **RQ4:** XSS is detected far better than RCE by learned models (p. 9), and SQLi per-class F1 is ≤ 0.146 (p. 9, Table 7). This is a hint that rare classes are effectively undetected by small ML models on PHP.
207	  - **C5 (class balance):** the choice of negatives flips the majority class and the failure direction of the same RF model (p. 9).

18	# A Review of Source Code Vulnerability Detection Methods Based on Large Language Models: Models, Techniques, and Evaluation
19	
20	- Authors: Qin, Letong
21	- Year / venue: 2026, Computers and Artificial Intelligence (published) — **venue flag [I]:** published by Zeus Press (p. 1); no peer-review statement or received/accepted dates in the PDF (pp. 1–16); low-visibility source not in DOAJ (OpenAlex, 2026-11-12). Peer review is not documented; weight like grey literature (see Analyst notes).
22	- DOI: 10.70267/cai.v3n5.122137 · URL: https://doi.org/10.70267/cai.v3n5.122137
23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
24	
25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
26	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
27	
28	## 1. Research objective
29	- [A] Review source-code vulnerability detection with "lightweight code Transformers and large-scale language models" as the two lines of discussion, covering input construction, task adaptation, use of program-analysis information and multi-model collaboration, and compare them by datasets, metrics and deployment conditions (p. 1).
30	- [A] Scope is limited to source-code-level detection, localization and classification; network intrusion, malware, smart contracts, vulnerability generation and automatic repair are excluded (p. 1).
31	
32	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
33	- [A] Three organising questions in the introduction: what capabilities methods actually improve, under what data conditions/protocols the gains are obtained, and whether evidence suffices for real-world deployment (p. 2).
34	- [A] Four formal RQs: RQ1 development from sequence/graph models to code pretraining and LLM interaction; RQ2 performance evidence of direct prompting, in-context learning, fine-tuning, structural enhancement and multi-model collaboration; RQ3 effects of label noise, duplication, class imbalance and temporal leakage; RQ4 how cross-project, out-of-time, false-positive-cost, localization and explanation evaluation approach deployment (p. 4).
35	- [I] The two framings are not reconciled: the introduction organises the paper around "three closely related questions" (p. 2), while Section 3.1 sets four formal RQs (p. 4), and the paper does not map one onto the other. Separately, it gives "medium confidence to C2" (p. 12), but no claim labelled C1/C2 is defined anywhere in the text.
36	
37	## 3. Methodology
38	- Research design: [I] Narrative (traditional) review. The paper calls itself a "review" (p. 1) and gives no search strategy, databases, search strings, date window, inclusion/exclusion screening, PRISMA flow, or study-quality assessment — all "not reported". The only inclusion rule stated is that it "includes only studies that directly analyze source code" and excludes repair (p. 4).
39	- Approach / taxonomy: [A] Methods are classified "by how vulnerability knowledge is acquired" rather than by model scale, core technology or supply-chain stage as in earlier reviews (p. 4). Two routes: (a) lightweight code Transformers — code pretraining + supervised fine-tuning, input granularity, structural fusion (pp. 5–6); (b) large-scale LLMs — supervised fine-tuning/steering, multitask learning, direct prompting, few-shot/ICL, hybrid detection with program analysis, ensembles/multi-model collaboration, explanation (pp. 6–9). Figure 1 adds cross-cutting layers "Data and bias", "Reliability evaluation" and "Discussion and outlook" (p. 3) [V, from figure].
40	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [A] Traditional methods (SAST, GNNs) are discussed "only in two situations": to motivate structural information for Transformers and as baselines or external tools for LLMs; "this paper does not provide a separate review of traditional detection methods" (p. 4). Section 7.1 nevertheless compares LLMs with DL and SAST qualitatively (pp. 11–12).
41	
42	## 4. Dataset and sample
43	- Data source(s): [V] Secondary literature; the reference list has 32 entries (pp. 14–16).
44	- Sample size (N) and unit: [I] No corpus size is stated; we counted 32 references (pp. 14–16), of which about 16 are LLM-based detection or evaluation studies (our count of the reference list). Table 1 lists 12 representative methods, 8 of them LLM-based (GRACE, EnStack, DLAP, fine-tuning LLM, LLMVulExp, cross-project zero-shot, context-enhanced, M2CVD; pp. 6–7). Several references are themselves reviews/surveys [2–4, 18–21] (pp. 14–15).
45	- Sampling / selection method: not reported. [I] Reference years run 2019–2026 (pp. 14–16), but no time window is stated. Figure 2 places milestones from 2019 (Devign) to 2026 (context enhancement, M2CVD) (p. 4) [V, from figure].
46	- Data availability: not applicable / not reported (no extraction sheet or study list released).
47	
48	## 5. Experimental setup
49	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: not applicable (no experiments). [A] One quantitative re-report (no new analysis): the review restates PrimeVul Table V for five code LMs — BigVul train/test F1 62.88%–68.26%, BigVul→PrimeVul F1 1.91%–5.82%, PrimeVul train/test F1 18.05%–21.43%, VD-S 88.78%–91.51%, paired-both-correct 1.06%–3.01%, paired-both-benign 84.22%–88.30% (p. 12). [I] We checked all six ranges against the primary source: they match Table V [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7]. For evidence, cite ding2025vulnerability directly, not this review.
50	- Code availability: not applicable.
51	
52	## 6. Evaluation metrics
53	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: [A] The review recommends reporting at least Precision, Recall, F1 and a confusion matrix, grouped by project, time, language or CWE; Top-k and audit effort at fixed recall for localization; separate checks of location/type/cause/suggestion for explanations; Accuracy only as supplementary; mean, fluctuation range and parse-failure rate for repeated LLM calls (p. 11). It re-reports VD-Score and paired metrics from PrimeVul (p. 11) and Top-10 Accuracy/Effort@20%Recall from LineVul (p. 5).
54	- Statistical testing: not applicable; the review does no pooling, meta-analysis or effect-size synthesis (not reported).
55	
56	## 7. Key findings
57	1. Benchmark inflation — [A] Gains from code pretraining, prompting, fine-tuning and structural enhancement hold "on specific benchmarks" but are "easily affected by duplicate samples, label noise, random splits, temporal leakage, and changes in model versions" (p. 1). Supported by the PrimeVul re-report (primary source: [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7]): StarCoder2 F1 68.26% on BigVul vs 3.09% on the PrimeVul test set (p. 2) and the five-model ranges above (p. 12).
58	2. Random-split F1 should be called "within-benchmark performance", not a real-world detection rate; out-of-time testing should be a reliability baseline, combined with project isolation and reporting of time windows, data-freeze dates and model knowledge cutoffs (p. 10) — [A].
59	3. Contamination from pretraining corpora is treated "as an alternative explanation that needs to be audited", not a confirmed fact; knowledge-cutoff dates are not proof of no contamination (p. 10) — [A].
60	4. Cross-study ranking is not possible: GRACE, DLAP, context enhancement and M2CVD "all report gains in their own settings, but datasets, model versions, and evaluation protocols differ, so they cannot be directly ranked" (p. 12) — [A]. [A] Table 2 is a normative risk matrix (the author's recommendations, not data): label noise, exact/near duplicates, pretraining contamination, random splitting, cross-project/language failure, class imbalance, false-positive cost, explanation/version validity, each with identification signals and mitigations (pp. 10–11).
61	5. LLM vs SAST vs DL — [A] "SAST is usually more stable within the scope covered by existing rules, whereas LLMs are better at semantic summarization and alert explanation"; unified benchmarks "support complementarity rather than complete replacement", with the two tool types finding different vulnerabilities and different false positives (p. 12). It cites [1] and [15]. [1] is a SAST-only study of query-based C/C++ tools (p. 14); [15] is the Gnieciak & Szandala LLM-vs-SAST benchmark (p. 15), its only head-to-head source. No numbers for this comparison are given. [I] Qin leaves out that [15] found LLMs above SAST on mean F1 (0.75–0.80 vs 0.26–0.55) [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10]. "SAST is usually more stable" is therefore not supported by its own cited comparison. Cite gnieciak2025large directly for this comparison.
62	6. Hybrids — [A] Proposed workflow: "SAST candidate generation-LLM review or explanation-human confirmation" (p. 8), to be judged by audit time, false-negative control and explanation consistency rather than overall F1 (p. 8); outputs should not be "simply concatenate[d]" (p. 13). Evidence cited is GRACE (structure + ICL, ≥28.65% relative F1 gain over six baselines, p. 8), DLAP (DL-augmented prompting, p. 8) and the context-enhancement study [29] (p. 8). No quantitative evidence on SAST+LLM hybrids is reported.
63	7. Cost — [A] API calls, GPU memory, latency, model updates and prompt maintenance should be counted; sensitive code and local large-scale scanning suit lightweight models or SAST; high-risk scenarios should use hybrid workflows with human confirmation (p. 12). No cost figures are reported.
64	8. Re-reported primary numbers (all [A], from cited papers): LineVul 188k+ functions, F1 +160%–379% over baselines, Top-10 Accuracy +12%–25%, Effort@20%Recall −29%–53% (p. 5); DiverseVul 7,514 commits, 18,945 vulnerable / 330,492 non-vulnerable functions, 150 CWEs (p. 9); LLMVulExp average F1 92.4% on SeVC single-type setting (p. 8).
65	
66	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
67	- [A] No separate limitations section. Scope exclusions: network intrusion, malware, smart contracts, generation, repair (p. 1).
68	- [A] Traditional detection methods are not reviewed separately (p. 4).
69	- [A] Specific caveats on cited evidence: the PrimeVul conclusion "is limited to the five models and three settings in Table V" (p. 12); LLMVulExp results "cannot be directly generalized to PrimeVul, cross-project testing, or real deployment" (pp. 8–9); GRACE gain is relative and applies only to the tested configurations (p. 8).
70	
71	## 9. Limitations we identified
72	- [I] Not systematic: no search protocol, databases, screening, corpus count or quality assessment (absence across pp. 1–4). Its conclusions cannot be checked for selection bias, and it cannot be cited as a systematic review.
73	- [I] Small and selective corpus (32 references, pp. 14–16). Missing, among others, project-scale LLM/SAST studies and LLM-based SAST-alarm filtering work that we have (e.g. li2026llm, du2026reducing, xiong2026sifting, li2024iris, guo2025repoaudit); hybrid claims rest on GRACE, DLAP and one context-enhancement study (p. 8), not on SAST+LLM evaluations.
74	- [I] SAST is explicitly out of scope (p. 4), yet the review draws an LLM-vs-SAST conclusion (p. 12) from two references [1, 15] with no numbers. Only [15] compares the two families, and it favours LLMs on F1 [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10]. That conclusion is under-supported.
75	- [I] Contradictions are explained only in general terms. Apart from the PrimeVul Table V re-reading (p. 12), it does not tabulate conflicting results from different studies side by side against their evaluation setups (benchmark, split, class ratio, granularity). Table 1 (pp. 6–7) is qualitative: no numbers, no split type per study.
76	- [I] Cites PrimeVul as a 2024 arXiv preprint (p. 15) and leans heavily on that one study for the inflation argument.
77	- [I] Editorial loose ends (the three framing questions on p. 2 are not reconciled with the four formal RQs on p. 4; "C2" on p. 12 is undefined) suggest light editorial review (see Analyst notes on venue).
78	
79	## 10. Threats to validity
80	- Internal (selection): [I] Unknown selection process, so selection bias cannot be judged; the reviewer's framing (evaluation pitfalls) may have driven which studies were cited.
81	- External: [I] Mostly C/C++ function-level benchmarks (BigVul, PrimeVul, DiverseVul, SeVC, ReVeal, FFmpeg+Qemu; pp. 8–9, 12); multilingual evidence is one reference [32] (p. 13).
82	- Source dependence: [I] Its quantitative claims rest on a handful of cited studies, mainly PrimeVul [14] for benchmark inflation (pp. 2, 12) and Gnieciak & Szandala [15] for LLM vs SAST (p. 12). Both are already in our corpus (ding2025vulnerability, gnieciak2025large). Counting this review as extra support for the same claims would double-count them.
83	- Construct: [I] Good conceptual separation of label correctness, localization and explanation evidence (p. 4); recommends metrics beyond F1 (p. 11).
84	- Statistical conclusion: [I] No quantitative synthesis; confidence levels ("medium confidence to C2", p. 12) are given without a stated grading scheme.
85	- Reproducibility: [I] Not reproducible as a review (no protocol, no study list beyond references).
86	
87	## 11. Future research directions
88	- Stated by authors [A]: traceable data pipelines with commit, time, label-source and duplicate statistics and updateable data cards (p. 13); out-of-time and project-isolated testing as main evidence, random splits only for historical comparison (p. 13); uncertainty calibration, risk-coverage curves and recall at a fixed false-positive budget (p. 13); decomposed verification of explanations (location, trigger, path, CWE, fix) (p. 13); human-machine studies recording audit time per real vulnerability (p. 13); SAST-LLM systems that measure candidate recall, LLM filtering gain, explanation correctness and total audit cost separately (p. 13); preserving system prompts, model IDs, call dates, temperatures and repetition counts (p. 13).
89	- Suggested by us [I]: a systematic, protocol-based review that puts SAST, DL and LLM results on the same evaluation-setup axes. This is exactly the gap between this review and ours.
90	
91	## 12. Relevance to our research
92	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ2 (primary), RQ3 (conceptual only), RQ1 (qualitative only), RQ5.
93	- How it informs our work [I]: This is the closest competing review and must be cited for positioning. Overlap: evaluation-reliability framing (duplicates, label noise, temporal splits, contamination) and the SAST-LLM-human workflow recommendation. Difference: it is narrative, has a small corpus (32 references), explicitly excludes SAST as a reviewed family, gives no quantitative LLM-vs-SAST or hybrid evidence, and does not map contradictions study-by-study onto evaluation setup. Our contribution should be stated against those four points. Its recommendations agree with our RQ2 answer, but they do not corroborate it independently: qin cites ding2025vulnerability [14], gnieciak2025large [15] and sheng2025llms [21] (p. 15), which are all in our corpus. Weak strength; use it for positioning only.
94	
95	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
96	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
97	|---|---|---|---|---|
98	| RQ2 | Benchmark gains are inflated by duplicates, label noise, random splits, temporal leakage and model-version changes; random-split F1 = "within-benchmark performance" only | 1, 10 | A | weak (narrative review) |
99	| RQ2 | Re-reports PrimeVul Table V: five code LMs F1 62.88–68.26% on BigVul vs 1.91–5.82% BigVul→PrimeVul vs 18.05–21.43% PrimeVul→PrimeVul; all ranges match the primary source [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7] — cite ding directly | 12 | A | weak (secondary re-report; not independent of ding2025vulnerability) |
100	| RQ2 | LLM methods (GRACE, DLAP, context enhancement, M2CVD) cannot be ranked because datasets, model versions and protocols differ | 12 | A | weak |
101	| RQ1 | SAST more stable within rule coverage; LLMs better at semantic summarisation/explanation; unified benchmarks support complementarity, not replacement (no numbers; its only head-to-head source found LLMs above SAST on F1 [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10]) | 12 | A | weak |
102	| RQ3 | Recommends SAST candidates → LLM ranking/explanation → human confirmation; judge by audit time, false negatives, explanation consistency, not F1 | 8, 13 | A | weak (no quantitative hybrid evidence) |
103	| RQ3 | Costs (API calls, GPU memory, latency, version drift, prompt maintenance) should be reported; none quantified | 9, 12 | A | weak |
104	| RQ5 | Open problems: out-of-time + project-isolated testing, data cards, uncertainty calibration, fixed-FP-budget recall, explanation verification, audit-time studies | 13 | A | weak |
105	
106	## 14. Key quotes
107	> "this paper does not provide a separate review of traditional detection methods" (p. 4)
108	
109	> "Existing evidence from unified benchmarks supports complementarity rather than complete replacement by one tool" (p. 12)
110	
111	> "F1 obtained from a random split should be called “within-benchmark performance” and cannot be directly described as a “real-world detection rate”" (p. 10)
112	
113	## Analyst notes
114	- Reading coverage: all 16 PDF pages read in full, including references, funding and copyright notes (pp. 14–16). Figures 1–2 (pp. 3–4) read from the PDF images because pdftotext dropped them.
115	- Venue quality [I]: Computers and Artificial Intelligence, Vol. 3 No. 5 (2026), E-ISSN 3006-3728, published by "Zeus Press" (p. 1). The PDF has no received/revised/accepted dates and no editor or peer-review statement (pp. 1–16). OpenAlex (queried 2026-11-12) lists the source with no host organisation, `is_in_doaj: false`, `is_core: false`, no indexing lists, and publication date 2026-10-29; cited_by 0 in metadata. The acknowledgment reads only "This paper is an output of the science project." (p. 16). There is a single author, and editorial loose ends remain (framing questions not reconciled with the formal RQs; "C2" undefined). Together these are warning signs of a low-visibility venue with uncertain peer review. We did not confirm that it is predatory. Treat it as tier 1 by `venue_kind` but weight it like grey literature. Cite it for positioning, not as evidence.
116	- Competitor positioning [I]: SAST tools are covered only as baselines/external tools, not reviewed (p. 4). Hybrids are covered conceptually (pp. 8, 13), with no SAST+LLM empirical studies. Cross-study contradictions are explained via evaluation setup in general terms and through one worked example (PrimeVul, p. 12), not systematically.
117	- Uncertainties: whether a systematic search was done but simply not reported. Numbers it gives for other papers are labelled [A] here; only the PrimeVul numbers (all six ranges, ding2025vulnerability Table V, p. 7) and the cited LLM-vs-SAST result (gnieciak2025large, p. 10) were cross-checked against a primary text.
118	- Review fixes 2026-11-12 (critical review C, findings 1–9): PrimeVul re-report relabelled [A] and its evidence row downgraded to weak; Table 1 count corrected to 12 methods (8 LLM-based); [1] identified as SAST-only, and the omitted gnieciak F1 result added; "independent corroboration" removed; Table 2 relabelled [A] (normative); RQ-framing wording softened; venue flag added to header; source-dependence threat added.

- Inputs: 20 analyses (`status: complete`, all full text), `evidence-matrix.md`, `literature-matrix.md`, critical reviews A and B of 2026-11-12.
- Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data, **[A]** author claim, **[I]** our interpretation. Unlabelled numeric statements are [V] from the cited page.
- Source tiers: three items are recorded by `rlab` as arXiv preprints. IRIS [@li2024iris, p. 1] and RepoAudit [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 1] are the ICLR 2025 and ICML 2025 camera-ready texts. Only zhou2024comparison is a true preprint without a known peer-reviewed version (**not peer-reviewed**) [@zhou2024comparison, p. 1]. Of the other 17 papers, 15 were read from arXiv copies rather than the version of record; only tan2026think and yildiz2025benchmarking were read in publisher form (see §5, W9).

A short glossary for readers new to the area: *SAST* (static application security testing) tools such as CodeQL or Semgrep scan code with hand-written rules. *DL detectors* (e.g. LineVul, Devign) are neural networks trained on labelled vulnerable code. A *balanced* test set has 50% vulnerable samples. *Pairwise correctness (P-C / pAcc)* is the share of vulnerable/patched function pairs where both versions are classified correctly. *SFDR* is the sampled false discovery rate, i.e. the share of a tool's warnings that are false.

A short glossary for readers new to the area:
- *SAST* (static application security testing) tools such as CodeQL or Semgrep scan code with hand-written rules.
- *DL detectors* (e.g. LineVul, Devign) are neural networks trained on labelled vulnerable code.
- *Prevalence* is the share of vulnerable samples in a test set. A *balanced* test set has 50% vulnerable samples; real code has far fewer (about 2% in two pass-2 studies).
- A *trivial baseline* is a classifier that ignores the code, for example "always vulnerable", "always safe" (majority class) or a rule based only on function length.
- *Balanced accuracy* is the mean of the recall on vulnerable and on safe samples, so every trivial baseline scores 0.5.
- *Pairwise correctness (P-C / pAcc)* is the share of vulnerable/patched function pairs where both versions are classified correctly. lu2025lab calls the same idea *patch pair accuracy (PACC)*.
- *SFDR* is the sampled false discovery rate, i.e. the share of a tool's warnings that are false.
- *Out-of-distribution (OOD)* test data come from a different source or time period than the training data.

General coding agents reach far higher recall than SAST [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 9]. [I] The family's main weakness is that each study uses its own targets and scoring, so the papers measure different things (see §3.5).

**B. LLM vs fine-tuned DL/PLM.** On random-split Big-Vul, fine-tuned small models clearly beat prompted ChatGPT (F1 94% vs 29%) [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4]. Under realistic splits all models collapse [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7; @chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 7]. The only multilingual comparison finds that the winner depends on class balance [@shu2026evaluating, p. 17; @shu2026evaluating, p. 40]. [I] This family inherits the label noise and leakage of Big-Vul-type data (§5, W2).
input.new_string:
General coding agents reach far higher recall than SAST [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 9]. deininger2026open scores both families on the same 1549 PrimeVul functions. Seven of eight zero-shot LLMs (balanced accuracy 0.604–0.676) score above the best lightweight SAST configuration (Flawfinder 0.589, Cppcheck up to 0.592; Semgrep 0.501–0.514) [@deininger2026open, p. 7; @deininger2026open, p. 10]. At the natural 1:44 prevalence, however, Flawfinder and Semgrep are more precise than every LLM [@deininger2026open, p. 8; @deininger2026open, p. 10]. Its SAST arm has no CodeQL, because isolated functions cannot be built [@deininger2026open, p. 10]. [I] The family's main weakness is that each study uses its own targets and scoring, so the papers measure different things (see §3.5).

**B. LLM vs fine-tuned DL/PLM.** On random-split Big-Vul, fine-tuned small models clearly beat prompted ChatGPT (F1 94% vs 29%) [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4]. Under realistic splits all models collapse [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7; @chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 7]. The only multilingual comparison finds that the winner depends on class balance [@shu2026evaluating, p. 17; @shu2026evaluating, p. 40]. Two pass-2 studies add:
- On unpaired PrimeVul functions, a fine-tuned 125M CodeBERT beats all eight zero-shot LLMs (balanced accuracy 0.765 vs ≤ 0.711) [@deininger2026open, p. 11; @deininger2026open, p. 17]. With a default 0.5 decision threshold, the same detector looks like an always-safe classifier [@deininger2026open, p. 11].
- On 2025 CVEs (VentiVul), trained DL detectors reach F1 3.47–8.65 and four open LLMs ≤ 32B reach conservative F1 0.79–5.36 [@lu2025lab, p. 13; @lu2025lab, p. 14]. [I] Both are close to the all-positive F1 of about 3.87%.

[I] This family inherits the label noise and leakage of Big-Vul-type data (§5, W2). Its results also depend on the decision threshold and the test prevalence (C1, C5, C8).

**B2. SAST vs classical ML/DL without an LLM.** tashenova2026real is the only PHP study in the corpus. On real WordPress plugin CVEs, an unnamed in-house intra-procedural lexical taint analyser detects 1.7–1.8% of vulnerabilities [@tashenova2026real, p. 9]. The authors say this low recall reflects "that implementation rather than taint analysis in general" [@tashenova2026real, p. 13] [A]. The best learned model reaches macro-F1 0.601, and no neural model leads in any of six settings [@tashenova2026real, p. 8]. [I] The paper says nothing about LLMs and cannot stand for established PHP SAST tools.

A word-count classifier reaches F1 0.86 on BigVul [@risse2025top, p. 11]. Statement-level scoring halves LLM F1 [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 8].

**F. Surveys.** Two SLRs and one narrative survey describe a field dominated by function-level C/C++ classification on noisy datasets [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 26; @zhou2025large, p. 18; @sheng2025llms, p. 20]. None pools effect sizes. kaniewski2026systematic excludes studies that only post-process tool output [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 8], so it does not cover family C2.
input.new_string:
A word-count classifier reaches F1 0.86 on BigVul [@risse2025top, p. 11]. Statement-level scoring halves LLM F1 [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 8]. The pass-2 papers add three things:
- **Label audit outside C/C++.** An expert review finds only 48.8% of cleaned positive WordPress-PHP labels genuine (single annotator, n = 400) [@tashenova2026real, p. 11]. A one-feature token-count baseline matches or beats TF-IDF Random Forest in 4 of 6 settings [@tashenova2026real, p. 8].
- **Temporal separation.** VentiVul uses CVEs disclosed from May 2025, with the sample size fixed before collection [@lu2025lab, p. 4].
- **Realistic prevalence.** deininger re-scores all detectors at PrimeVul's natural 1:44 ratio [@deininger2026open, p. 8].

**F. Surveys and reviews.** Two SLRs and two narrative reviews describe a field dominated by function-level C/C++ classification on noisy datasets [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 26; @zhou2025large, p. 18; @sheng2025llms, p. 20; @qin2026review, p. 12]. None pools effect sizes. kaniewski2026systematic excludes studies that only post-process tool output [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 8], so it does not cover family C2.

qin2026review is a single-author narrative review with 32 references and no search protocol [@qin2026review, p. 14]. Its quantitative claims re-report ding2025vulnerability and gnieciak2025large [@qin2026review, p. 12], so it is not independent support for either. It concludes that SAST is "usually more stable" within rule coverage [@qin2026review, p. 12] [A]. [I] Its only head-to-head source, however, found LLMs above SAST on F1 [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10]. We use qin2026review only to position our review.

### 3.7 Agreements / converging evidence
input.new_string:
li2026llm uses recall on known CVEs and SFDR on new code [@li2026llm, p. 11]. deininger2026open scores LLMs and SAST on identical functions with identical metrics (balanced accuracy and precision at 1:44) [@deininger2026open, p. 10]. Within that one study, the comparison is like-for-like. Its SAST arm is lightweight, though: Flawfinder, Cppcheck and Semgrep, with no CodeQL [@deininger2026open, p. 10]. [I] These six studies cannot be pooled or ranked against each other. tashenova2026real reports macro-F1 on PHP for a bespoke analyser [@tashenova2026real, p. 8] and does not add to this comparison.

**3.6 False-positive filtering (not numerically comparable).** du measures removal of false alarms on 433 industrial alarms of general bug types [@du2026reducing, p. 8]. xiong measures residual FPR and TP miss rate on OWASP and 100 sampled alerts [@xiong2026sifting, p. 12; @xiong2026sifting, p. 18]. Only the qualitative pattern can be compared (§3.9, G7).

**3.7 Unpaired PrimeVul functions vs PrimeVul pairs (not comparable; do not pool).** The two designs differ as follows:
- **deininger** samples 1549 single functions (35.4% vulnerable) from the PrimeVul test split [@deininger2026open, p. 4]. It reports balanced accuracy 0.511–0.711 for LLMs and 0.765 for fine-tuned CodeBERT [@deininger2026open, p. 7; @deininger2026open, p. 11; @deininger2026open, p. 17].
- **ding, tan and yildiz** score both members of each vulnerable/patched pair together (§3.2).

The unit, prevalence and metric all differ. [I] Balanced accuracy on single functions and pair-wise correctness answer different questions. The first asks whether a detector ranks vulnerable functions above safe ones. The second asks whether it notices the fix. So "fine-tuned CodeBERT beats all LLMs" (deininger) and "GPT-4 beats fine-tuned models on pairs" (ding) are not a numerical contradiction; C1 discusses them. Even inside one study, yildiz's F1 drops from ~49–65% on balanced pairs to 5.41–12.21% on non-paired PrimeVul [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 7]. deininger's PrimeVul test split (24,788 functions, 549 vulnerable) also differs from the split recorded by ding (695 vulnerable / 25,216 benign) [@deininger2026open, p. 4; @ding2025vulnerability, p. 6]. deininger explains this only as "after loading".

**3.8 Detection at realistic prevalence (not numerically comparable; same direction).** Two studies score detectors at about 2% prevalence against a trivial baseline:
- **deininger** (PrimeVul, 1:44 ≈ 2.2%): every LLM's precision is 2.3–3.8% in the first epoch and 2.8–4.6% in the budget-matched epoch, vs 2.21% for flag-all [@deininger2026open, p. 8; @deininger2026open, p. 17].
- **lu** (VentiVul, 1.97% [I]): trained DL reaches F1 3.47–8.65, and 7 of 12 LLM conservative F1 values fall below the all-positive F1 of about 3.87% [@lu2025lab, p. 13; @lu2025lab, p. 14].

The datasets, metrics (precision vs F1) and models differ (frontier and open LLMs vs open LLMs ≤ 32B). [I] Both show LLMs only slightly above, or below, a classifier that flags everything.

### 3.9 Agreements / converging evidence

Numbering follows the "Agreements" section of `evidence-matrix.md`.

**C7. Same model, same benchmark, different in-distribution score: lu2025lab vs ding2025vulnerability.**
- Claim A: LineVul (CodeBERT) trained and tested on BigVul reaches F1 91.00 [@lu2025lab, p. 12].
- Claim B: CodeBERT trained and tested on BigVul reaches F1 62.88 [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7].
- Differences: neither paper explains the 28-point gap. lu used LineVul's original pipeline and recommended settings [@lu2025lab, p. 8]. ding's split and preprocessing are its own.
- [I] Explanation: likely split and preprocessing differences. In-distribution BigVul numbers are not comparable across papers (§3.3).

**C8. Does a time-split fine-tuned detector survive? deininger2026open vs lu2025lab.**
- Claim A: CodeBERT-PrimeVul keeps balanced accuracy 0.765 on PrimeVul's chronologically later test split [@deininger2026open, p. 11]. At 1:44 prevalence this corresponds to F1 ≈ 0.15 (our calculation from reported TPR and precision).
- Claim B: DL trained on BigVul, ICVul, Devign or Juliet falls to F1 3.47–8.65 on post-May-2025 VentiVul [@lu2025lab, p. 13].
- Differences:
  - test data: PrimeVul functions with CVEs from 2008–2022 [@deininger2026open, p. 24] vs VentiVul 2025 CVEs scored per function across whole files [@lu2025lab, p. 4];
  - training data: PrimeVul's own training split vs older, noisier benchmarks;
  - threshold policy: validation-tuned [@deininger2026open, p. 11] vs the original implementations' settings [@lu2025lab, p. 8];
  - metric: balanced accuracy vs F1.
- [I] Explanation: unresolved. A detector trained on cleaner data from the same source, with a tuned threshold, may hold up better than detectors trained on other benchmarks. Neither study tests this directly.

input.old_string:
- **W1. F1 on balanced data without a trivial baseline.** On a 50/50 set, "flag everything" scores F1 0.667. Examples:
  - shu's DummyClf_vul scores 0.6693 against a best of 0.7075 [@shu2026evaluating, p. 17].
  - tan's best F1 is 0.665–0.666 [@tan2026think, p. 7; @tan2026think, p. 11].
  - All of yildiz's GPT F1 values (48–66) are at or below it [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 6].
  - khare's best-per-dataset F1s include always-vulnerable rows [@khare2025understanding, p. 16].

  [I] Only shu reports the baseline itself.
- **W2. Label noise and leakage.** Exact-copy test-to-train leakage reaches 12.7% (BigVul) and 18.9% (CVEFixes) [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4]. Benchmarks probably sit in LLM pre-training data [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 30] [A]. Only xiong and li2026llm test explicitly on post-cutoff code [@xiong2026sifting, p. 15; @li2026llm, p. 5]. shu adds a time split [@shu2026evaluating, p. 39].
input.new_string:
- **W1. Trivial baselines rarely reported.** On a 50/50 set, "flag everything" scores F1 0.667, so balanced-data F1 near that value shows no skill. Examples:
  - shu's DummyClf_vul scores 0.6693 against a best of 0.7075 [@shu2026evaluating, p. 17].
  - tan's best F1 is 0.665–0.666 [@tan2026think, p. 7; @tan2026think, p. 11].
  - All of yildiz's GPT F1 values (48–66) are at or below it [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 6].
  - khare's best-per-dataset F1s include always-vulnerable rows [@khare2025understanding, p. 16].

  Pass 2 shows the same problem at other prevalences (G10):
  - deininger: the best LLM F1 (0.615) is 0.092 above always-vulnerable (0.523), and Qwen3-Coder-30B (0.405) is below it [@deininger2026open, p. 7].
  - tashenova: a token-count baseline is within 0.006 of the best neural model [@tashenova2026real, p. 8].
  - lu reports no trivial baseline. [I] By our calculation, 7 of its 12 LLM conservative F1 values fall below the all-positive F1 of about 3.87% [@lu2025lab, p. 14].

  [I] Only shu, deininger and tashenova report trivial-classifier baselines (3 of 19 primary studies). ding reports a random reference only for pair-wise correctness [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9]. tashenova's authors argue that detectors should be required to clear such baselines [@tashenova2026real, p. 13] [A].
- **W2. Label quality and leakage.** Problems include:
  - **Exact-copy leakage** from test to train reaches 12.7% (BigVul) and 18.9% (CVEFixes) [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4]. Even plugin-grouped PHP folds contained duplicate groups spanning folds (166 / 151 groups) and 730 / 456 groups with contradictory labels before cleaning [@tashenova2026real, p. 4].
  - **Label quality** is low wherever it is audited: 39–65% [@risse2025top, p. 8], 24–36% [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4] and 48.8% for PHP [@tashenova2026real, p. 11] of positive labels are correct. [I] tashenova's evaluated corpus also contains lower-tier labels, so its true label precision is probably lower still. Its authors call label quality, not architecture, "the binding constraint" [@tashenova2026real, p. 12] [A].
  - **Contamination.** Benchmarks probably sit in LLM pre-training data [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 30] [A]. deininger finds recall 7–15 points higher on pre-2020 than on 2021–2022 CVEs for better-balanced LLMs, which is consistent with memorisation [@deininger2026open, p. 24].
  - **Post-cutoff testing** is rare. Only xiong, li2026llm and lu test explicitly on code disclosed after the evaluated models' release [@xiong2026sifting, p. 15; @li2026llm, p. 5; @lu2025lab, p. 5]. lu notes that release-date separation cannot fully exclude contamination [@lu2025lab, p. 17]. shu adds a time split [@shu2026evaluating, p. 39].

input.new_string:
- **W5. Single runs, no statistics.** Most studies report one run of non-deterministic models without variance (§1). Examples:
  - zhou2024's results rest on about 8–10 test CVEs per language [I] [@zhou2024comparison, p. 6].
  - xiong's real-world samples are 50 alerts each [@xiong2026sifting, p. 13].
  - shu chooses the best of ~30 configurations post hoc [@shu2026evaluating, p. 17].
  - lu runs each LLM once and does not report DL run counts [@lu2025lab, p. 8].
  - tashenova uses a single seed [@tashenova2026real, p. 7].

  deininger shows why this matters. A reworded prompt moves balanced accuracy by up to 0.088 and changes which model wins [@deininger2026open, p. 19; @deininger2026open, p. 20]. Absolute scores shift by up to 0.06 between measurement epochs seven weeks apart [@deininger2026open, p. 20].
- **W6. Little cost reporting; energy figures of mixed provenance.** Twelve of 19 primary studies report no monetary cost (§1). Where cost is measured it is decisive: up to $1,247.66 per project [@li2026llm, p. 16]. Only deininger reports cost per true positive (G11), and it excludes human triage [@deininger2026open, p. 8]. Its energy figures mix three sources:
  - Frontier-model energy is a FLOP estimate that assumes 100B active parameters [@deininger2026open, p. 7].
  - The kJ per TP for Gemma, Qwen and Llama come from FLOP estimates (64, 40 and 944 J per task), not from measured energy [@deininger2026open, p. 8; @deininger2026open, p. 14].
  - The FLOP estimator overstates measured batched energy by 5.4–16.9× [@deininger2026open, p. 14].

  [I] With measured single-request energy, our recalculation gives about 4.9 (Gemma), 8.8 (Qwen) and 34.9 (Llama) kJ per TP. The ordering among open models changes, but the gap to frontier models remains. Energy numbers should always state whether they are measured or estimated.
- **W7. Narrow scope.** Data are C/C++-biased and long-tailed, and 555 mappable CWEs appear in no analysed dataset [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 34]. 87 studies build custom datasets and only nine datasets are reused in more than ten studies [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 35]. Only one of 40 detection studies to March 2024 worked at repository level [@zhou2025large, p. 18]. PHP is covered by a single function-level study, which has no LLM arm and only a bespoke analyser [@tashenova2026real, p. 13].
- **W8. Three-way comparisons are rare.** [I] Two studies evaluate LLMs, SAST and DL together:
  - khare, whose SAST arm covers synthetic data only [@khare2025understanding, p. 7];
  - deininger, on identical PrimeVul functions with lightweight SAST and no CodeQL [@deininger2026open, p. 10], using CVEs from 2008–2022 that predate the models' training cutoffs [@deininger2026open, p. 24].

  zhou2024 compares fine-tuned and prompted LLMs with SAST but no classic DL detector [@zhou2024comparison, p. 4]. lu compares DL with LLMs but has no SAST arm, and tashenova compares SAST with ML/DL but has no LLM arm [@lu2025lab, p. 7; @tashenova2026real, p. 13].
- **W9. Preprint text vs version of record.** Fifteen published papers were analysed from arXiv copies (xiong2026sifting's copy is the formatted published article). lu2025lab was read as the arXiv v4 accepted manuscript of its JSS 2026 version [@lu2025lab, p. 1]. du2026reducing comes from a v1 with a placeholder header [@du2026reducing, p. 2], so it has the highest risk that numbers changed. zhou2025large's only LLM-vs-SAST study is the authors' own zhou2024comparison [@zhou2025large, p. 22], so it is not independent support.
- **W10. Independence.** [I] Several sources overlap:
  - guo and li2026llm share five C/C++ modules.
  - ding, yildiz, tan and deininger all draw on PrimeVul.
  - Duplication figures reused elsewhere trace back to ding alone (critical review B).
  - qin2026review's quantitative claims re-report ding and gnieciak, so they add no independent support [@qin2026review, p. 12].
  - ICVul, one of lu's four training benchmarks, is the authors' own dataset [@lu2025lab, p. 3].
- **W11. Test prevalence rarely realistic.** Most test sets are balanced or close to it (W1), while vulnerable code is rare in practice. The pass-2 studies show what this hides:
  - Re-scored at PrimeVul's natural 1:44 ratio, LLMs raise 25.6–41.9 false positives per true one [@deininger2026open, p. 8].
  - At BigVul's 6% prevalence, DL accuracy of 87–94% hides F1 as low as 0.19 [@lu2025lab, p. 11].
  - tashenova draws negatives only from vulnerable plugins [@tashenova2026real, p. 3]. [I] Its prevalence is therefore 74.5% (Variant A) and 46.2% (Variant B), and the false-alarm rate in deployment is unknown.

  [I] Results from balanced sets should be re-scored at realistic prevalence before any deployment claim.

input.old_string:
- Status: answered (synthesis 2026-11-12)
- Current answer: No family wins across settings. I updated both synthesis files for pass 2. Both now cover 24 papers, and the citation check passes. I made all edits with Edit (plus one small `sed` fix to a section reference). I did not touch `gap-report.md`, `evidence-matrix.md`, `STATUS.md` or `research-log.md`.

Files changed:
- `/Users/makky/Downloads/AI-Research-Lab-main/research/2026-11-12-llm-based-vs-traditional-static-analysis/reports/methodology-comparison.md` (now ~8,900 words)
- `/Users/makky/Downloads/AI-Research-Lab-main/research/2026-11-12-llm-based-vs-traditional-static-analysis/RESEARCH-QUESTIONS.md`

## Changes to methodology-comparison.md
- **Header**
  - Counts now say 24 analyses and critical reviews A–D.
  - Source tiers: four records are arXiv preprints in `rlab`. `lu2025lab` is marked peer-reviewed (JSS 2026, doi 10.1016/j.jss.2026.113185), with page refs from arXiv v4.
  - `qin2026review` is flagged: Zeus Press venue, peer review not documented, weighted like grey literature, used for positioning only.
  - Of the other 20 papers, 15 were read from arXiv copies and 5 in publisher form.
  - The glossary adds prevalence, trivial baseline, balanced accuracy, PACC and OOD.
- **§1 Overview table**
  - Four new rows, in alphabetical order.
  - The summary line now says: 19 primary studies; significance tests only in tan and deininger (tashenova reports one test); 7 report cost; only shu, deininger and tashenova report trivial baselines.
- **§2 Approach families**
  - deininger added to A, B and E; lu to B and E; qin to F, renamed "Surveys and reviews".
  - New family B2 ("SAST vs classical ML/DL, no LLM") holds tashenova.
  - The A, B, E and F paragraphs are extended. The F paragraph says qin depends on ding and gnieciak and leaves out gnieciak's pro-LLM result.
- **§3 Comparable results**
  - lu's LineVul result (91.00) added to the Big-Vul comparison, with a pointer to C7.
  - §3.2 says deininger is excluded from the pairs comparison and that lu's PACC is related but comes from another dataset.
  - §3.5 adds deininger as the one like-for-like LLM-vs-SAST study, with lightweight SAST and no CodeQL.
  - New §3.7 "Unpaired PrimeVul (deininger) vs PrimeVul pairs (ding/tan/yildiz)" is marked **Not comparable; do not pool**. It also notes the split-size mismatch (549 vs 695 vulnerable functions).
  - New §3.8 compares realistic-prevalence results (deininger 1:44, lu 1.97%): not numerically comparable, but pointing the same way.
  - Agreements moved to §3.9 and **renumbered to match evidence-matrix G1–G11**. G5 "CodeQL on OWASP" is inserted; the old G5–G8 became G6–G9. G1 and G2 are extended, and G10 and G11 added, all worded as in the evidence matrix. Cross-references are updated.
- **§4 Contradictions**: C1, C3, C4 and C5 extended with the pass-2 text; C7 and C8 added. All are consistent with `evidence-matrix.md`.
- **§5 Weaknesses**
  - W1 is now "Trivial baselines rarely reported" (3 of 19 studies).
  - W2 is now "Label quality and leakage": tashenova's 48.8% labels and duplicate groups across folds, deininger's contamination gradient, lu's post-cutoff test and its caveat.
  - W5 adds prompt sensitivity (up to 0.088) and the 0.06 drift between epochs.
  - W6 is now "…energy figures of mixed provenance": FLOP estimates vs measured energy, our recalculation labelled [I], triage excluded.
  - W7 adds PHP, W8 now names two three-way studies, and W9 and W10 add lu and qin.
  - New W11 "Test prevalence rarely realistic".
- **§6 RQ answers** match `RESEARCH-QUESTIONS.md` and are split into bullets.

## New RQ1–RQ5 current answers (verbatim from RESEARCH-QUESTIONS.md)

**RQ1** — Current answer (updated pass 2, 2026-11-12): No family wins across settings. Frontier LLMs beat SAST on small, self-contained code [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10; @dubniczky2025castle, p. 11], but CodeQL beats LLMs on synthetic function-level suites [@khare2025understanding, p. 9]. At project scale general coding agents reach far higher recall than SAST (59.55% vs 0–34.29% on C/C++), while most LLM detectors and SAST tools produce mostly false warnings [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 11]. On the same 1549 unpaired PrimeVul functions, seven of eight zero-shot LLMs beat lightweight SAST on balanced accuracy [@deininger2026open, p. 7; @deininger2026open, p. 10]. At the natural 1:44 prevalence, however, Flawfinder and Semgrep are more precise than every LLM, whose precision (2.3–4.6%) is barely above flag-all (2.21%) [@deininger2026open, p. 8; @deininger2026open, p. 17]. Versus fine-tuned DL, the ranking depends on dataset, class balance and decision threshold [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4; @shu2026evaluating, p. 40; @deininger2026open, p. 11]. A fine-tuned CodeBERT beats all eight LLMs on those unpaired functions (balanced accuracy 0.765 vs ≤ 0.711) [@deininger2026open, p. 11; @deininger2026open, p. 17], and all families are near or below chance on PrimeVul pairs [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9; @tan2026think, p. 6]. On 2025 CVEs at 1.97% prevalence, trained DL (F1 3.47–8.65) and four open LLMs ≤ 32B (0.79–5.36) both sit near the all-positive F1 of about 3.87% [I] [@lu2025lab, p. 13; @lu2025lab, p. 14]. For PHP, no LLM has been tested; a bespoke lexical taint analyser detects 1.7–1.8% of vulnerabilities [@tashenova2026real, p. 9]. **Strength: weak–moderate.** Most results come from single-run studies with incompatible metrics, and only one study compares all three families on identical real functions, with lightweight SAST. Most robust pattern [I]: LLMs have higher recall and lower precision, and at realistic prevalence their margin over trivial baselines is small.

**RQ2** — Current answer (updated pass 2, 2026-11-12): Evaluation setup explains much of the disagreement. Sources of variation include:
- label noise: 39–65% of positive labels correct [@risse2025top, p. 8], and 48.8% in a PHP benchmark [@tashenova2026real, p. 11];
- leakage: exact-copy leakage up to 18.9% [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4], and duplicate and contradictory-label groups even across plugin-grouped folds [@tashenova2026real, p. 4];
- balanced vs realistic class ratios that flip rankings [@shu2026evaluating, p. 40; @yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 7; @deininger2026open, p. 8];
- trivial baselines that are rarely reported but often competitive [@tashenova2026real, p. 8; @deininger2026open, p. 7; @lu2025lab, p. 14];
- temporal and cross-dataset shift [@lu2025lab, p. 12; @lu2025lab, p. 13];
- prompt wording and decision threshold, either of which can change the winner [@deininger2026open, p. 11; @deininger2026open, p. 20];
- synthetic vs real code [@khare2025understanding, p. 5];
- function vs statement granularity [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 8];
- custom datasets with inconsistent splits [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 35]. The same model on the same named dataset can differ by 28 F1 points between papers [@lu2025lab, p. 12; @ding2025vulnerability, p. 7].

**Strength: strong** for label noise and the collapse under realistic evaluation, which are consistent across independent primary studies and two SLRs. **Moderate** for prompt and threshold sensitivity and for trivial baselines, which rest on fewer studies.

**RQ3** — Current answer (updated pass 2, 2026-11-12): LLM filtering of SAST alarms removes most false alarms at < $0.20 per alarm but loses 12–25% of real bugs [@du2026reducing, p. 8; @xiong2026sifting, p. 18] (**moderate**). Hybrid detection (IRIS, RepoAudit) beats SAST in the authors' own evaluations [@li2024iris, p. 8; @guo2025repoaudit, p. 8] but not in an independent project-scale study [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 12], and it needs a strong LLM [@li2024iris, p. 10] (**weak/contested**). LLM costs range from cents per alarm to $1,247.66 per project, against minutes and no token cost for SAST [@li2026llm, p. 16]. The only cost per true positive comes from a non-hybrid study: USD 0.003–0.212 and 3.7–119.6 kJ per true positive at 1:44 prevalence [@deininger2026open, p. 8]. These are compute costs only. Human triage of the 25.6–41.9 false positives per true one is excluded [@deininger2026open, p. 8], and part of the energy values are FLOP estimates [@deininger2026open, p. 14]. The same study finds that small open models can match a frontier model at 1/66 of the cost [@deininger2026open, p. 17] (**moderate, single study**). Explainability is limited: LLMs mislocate findings [@gnieciak2025large, p. 11], and fluent explanations do not signal correctness [@tan2026think, p. 9].

**RQ4** — Current answer (updated pass 2, 2026-11-12): LLMs do best on self-contained injection-style CWEs and worst on context-dependent and crypto/policy CWEs and on localising memory-safety bugs [@khare2025understanding, p. 7; @xiong2026sifting, p. 18; @shu2026evaluating, p. 30]. CodeQL is better on CWE-190 [@khare2025understanding, p. 8]. LLM performance falls with function/file length [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 13; @li2026llm, p. 9]. Results also vary by project: LineVul (BigVul) finds 76% of Chromium CVEs but none in Linux, while all LLMs cover Linux better [@lu2025lab, p. 13]. Evidence is concentrated on C/C++ and Java [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 28]. The only PHP evidence (tashenova2026real) tests no LLM and uses a bespoke lexical taint analyser that detects 1.7–1.8% of vulnerabilities. In that study, learned models detect XSS (F1 up to 0.500) far better than SQLi (≤ 0.146) or RCE (≤ 0.085) [@tashenova2026real, p. 9]. **Strength: weak** (small per-CWE cells, divergent results, a single PHP study).

**RQ5** — Current answer (updated pass 2, 2026-11-12): Recurring open problems:
- verified, realistic, repository-level benchmarks with context [@zhou2025large, p. 19; @sheng2025llms, p. 25];
- trivial baselines and realistic prevalence in every evaluation [@tashenova2026real, p. 13; @deininger2026open, p. 8];
- label quality and contamination control [@tashenova2026real, p. 12; @lu2025lab, p. 17];
- same-benchmark LLM vs SAST vs DL comparisons. Two studies run all three: khare, with SAST on synthetic data only [@khare2025understanding, p. 7], and deininger, with lightweight function-level SAST on pre-2023 CVEs [@deininger2026open, p. 10; @deininger2026open, p. 24];
- independent labelling and statistical testing, including prompt sensitivity [@li2026llm, p. 11; @deininger2026open, p. 20];
- cost reporting that includes human triage and states where energy figures come from [@deininger2026open, p. 8];
- true-positive loss in filtering [@xiong2026sifting, p. 19];
- workflow integration [@zhou2025large, p. 19].

deininger's authors judge that no tested method is ready for independent function-level triage [@deininger2026open, p. 26]. **Strength: moderate** [I]. These are candidate gaps only. Gap specifics and novelty checks are in gap-report.md.

Every Status line now reads "answered (synthesis 2026-11-12; updated pass 2, 2026-11-12)".

## Checks
- `rlab cite-check` on both files: **OK**. methodology-comparison.md has 421 citations covering all 24 papers; RESEARCH-QUESTIONS.md has 76 citations of 21 papers.
- `rlab bib`: references.bib has 24 entries.

## Claims left out or adjusted
- I checked quotes against `fulltext.txt`. tashenova says "the more plausible binding constraint" (p. 12), not "the binding constraint", so I quote it exactly that way.
- I did not extend G3 (over-flagging) or G4 (low SAST recall) with pass-2 data, because `evidence-matrix.md` does not. Two items could go there, both already cited elsewhere in the comparison:
  - G3: lu's PACC ≤ 5.75%, far below the random level.
  - G4: deininger's Semgrep recall of 0.002–0.031.
- I did not describe tan2026think's energy provenance, because its analysis does not record it. W6 discusses provenance for deininger only.
- I did not tick Synthesis in `STATUS.md`. It is still ticked from pass 1, and the orchestrator owns that file.
